utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we are going to resume our hearing. First, I would like to make sure that everything is working, that you can hear the interpretation. Everyone can hear me? The prosecuting counsel, the people in the visitors' gallery? I would like to hope that the interpreters have recovered from all the strain deployed yesterday, and we are going to try to catch up the time we lost yesterday. The Judges will be doing everything they can to see that we move ahead briskly. I suggest that we leave it like that and move right on to the substance of the matter. We are going to hear, prosecuting counsel, I am quite confident, our witness Professor Garde this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. We would like to resume with Professor Garde. PROFESSOR GARDE, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You are in tip-top shape, I trust? Great. So the prosecuting counsel is going to go on putting questions to you. You have the floor, prosecuting counsel. Examined by MR. BOWERS

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Garde.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we ended with your description of the rise of nationalism in the 1980s and a brief review of how the media reacted to that and influenced that. We would like to continue the chronology today. If you could pick up with where you left off and begin describing some of the events in the late 1980s and early 1990s that led up to the actual dissolution of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as the events in Serbia go, in the regions inhabited by Serbs, at the same time, that is, the second half of the 1980s, there was also the waning of communism in the north west Republics, and as of '86 little by little there was the appearance, it was anti-constitutional, but it was more or less tolerated, that there were parties emerging in Slovenia and there was a certain amount of democracy in that Republic. There was, of course, opposition with what was happening in Serbia because the Slovenes gave their backing to the Kosovo Albanians who were subjected to attacks from the Serbs. So, the conflict between these two Republics, Slovenia and Serbia, became quite acute, and particularly when the Slovenes banned a Serb rally that was to take place and the Serbians retaliated with an economic blockade against Slovenia, and a bit later the same movement of diversification on the political front, the fact that there were opposition parties that were tolerated, that also occurred in Croatia. Consequently, these two Republics were at odds with Serbia. Now, at that point in time, in 1989, there was the fall of communism in all the neighbouring countries, that is to say, the Berlin Wall came down and communism collapsed in Hungary, Bulgaria, etc, Rumania as well at one point or another, and the movement toward pluralism becomes a lot stronger, and the Yugoslav Republics could not disregard this general movement of liberalization. At that point in time there are various events that occurred. First, in early 1990 there is the break up of the communist party, the Yugoslav Communist League. The Slovenes and the Croats on the one hand and the Serbs on the other had taken opposite stances. At the party meeting in early 90, there was the dissolution and Slovenia left the congress followed by the Croats. That was it. That as end of the Yugoslav communist party. Subsequently, in the course of 1990, there were elections that took place first in the north west Republics, Slovenia Croatia, in the spring, in March/April 1990; whereas in the other Republics they took place in December. Now, in March in Slovenia and in Croatia those elections brought to power forces that were opposed to communism. In Croatia, in addition to that, the elections were won by a party that was quite nationalist, the HDZ of President Tudjman. Immediately, this coming to power of the nationalists in Croatia aggravated the tensions, because Croatia had a population of 12 per cent and they had already been affected by the campaigns, demonstrations, the threats, etc.. So they had this feeling and to an even greater extent was strengthened by propaganda. So, there was matter to feed such a campaign on the Croat side. One of the slogans was that the Serbs had too many important positions in the administration; so there was a dismissal of certain civil servants who were Serbian which, of course, reinforced their fears and their conviction that they were threatened. Similarly, there was a new constitution for Croatia that was adopted and, unlike the previous constitution which stated that Croatia was the state of both the Croat people and the Serbian Croat people, the new constitution said that Croatia was the state of the Croatian people, and of the other nationalities who lived there such as Serbs, Italians, Hungarians, etc. In other words, the Serbs in this new arrangement were moved out of the first category into the second category. So, they are second class citizens, as it were, even though the constitution granted to them all rights, at least in theory. But, in practice, they did not always actually possess those rights. Now, propaganda from Belgrade and the propaganda disseminated there among the Serbs of Croatia at that time, in particular that propaganda, as I already said yesterday, was constantly stressing the genocide of 1941, and in people's minds the idea is conveyed that genocide is going to happen again, and that this new Croatian government is picking up where the Ustasha left off. So, as of the summer of 1990, in the Serbian parts of Croatia there is some uprising. It starts off with roadblocks, and Croatian policemen were disarmed by Serbian insurgents. Then in the course of the following winter and spring, almost outright rebellion, the first deaths took place on 31st March 1991 at Plitvice. The first massacre that takes place on 2nd May 1991, that is, of Croatian policemen by Serbs, that is, on 2nd May 1991, Borovo Selo, 2nd May 1991, so two months practically before Croatia declared independence. The conflict was also deteriorating because Serbia had embezzled funds that were meant for Croatia. Then Serbia refused the right of the Croatian representative to be elected President. That was on 15th May 1991. There was the rotating Presidency. On 15th May 1991 the previous Serbian President's term came to an end. Normally, it was the Croatian who was the party of the nationalist Croatian party who was to succeed him. The representatives of the Serb block hindered that election. So there was no longer a Federal President, and the federal institutions were deadlocked. During that period the Slovenes and the Croatians were preparing their independence. There were referendums in December 1990 in Slovenia and then I believe it was in April or May '91, April or May 91, in May, in Croatia and people were very much in favour of independence. Those two countries on 25th June 1991 declared their independence and that was at that point in time that the federal army reacted, and that is when the military phase of the conflict begins, that is to say, with the federal army's intervention in Slovenia. That lasted just 10 days. The federal army's intervention and the war in Croatia lasted some six months, and later on in 1992 there would be the military intervention in Bosnia which has lasted until quite recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Garde. How did the declarations of independence in Slovenia and Croatia affect the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina, as we saw, is at the heart of the former Yugoslavia, and the people there, besides the Muslim Bosnians, you have Serbs and Croats there. Now, as a result, the setup in Yugoslavia suited the people in Bosnia, and survey showed that just before the war they were in favour of keeping their Yugoslav federation but on the condition that the federation be balanced, that is to say, that it included Serbia and Croatia as well. Bosnia was right in the middle and there was this desire of seeing this balance maintained, but once the federation no longer included Slovenia and Croatia, Bosnia ended up face to face, as it were, with Serbia and was on unequal terms because there was a lot more Serbs and they have a lot more power. So that solution whereby Bosnia would stay within the new Yugoslav federation that was dominated by the Serbs, well, alone amongst the people of Bosnia was the Serbs who were in favour of that and the Croats. The Muslims of Bosnia were very much against that. So, once the federation fell apart, the majority of the Bosnian population, since Muslims and Croats in Bosnia account for two-thirds of the population, so the majority of the population of Bosnia wanted at that point in time independence to be declared. In Bosnia at that time the elections in December 1990 had been won by the three nationalist parties, the SDS, Radovan Karadzic, that is, the Serbs; SDA of Alija Izetbegovic, that is the Muslim Bosnians and then the HDZ, the Croat party. So the three nationalist parties formed a coalition and ruled. They split up the authority, but that coalition did not last very long precisely because the various members of that coalition had conflicting interests. Two of the parties in question were for the independence of Bosnia; whereas as the third party, the SDS, the Serb party, was totally opposed to that. This is why the conflict came about in no time at all during the second half of 1991, that is to say, while the war was being waged in Croatia, the terrible war, in the course of which the Serbs army, the federal army with the help of the Yugoslav militia, occupied a third of Croatian territory, drove out the Croatians living there and already at the time there was ethnic cleansing going on. So whilst those events were occurring, Bosnia and Herzegovina remained outside of the conflict and, in principle, it was neutral, but President Izetbegovic was careful about that, but the federal army occupied the territory and it was used as a real base against Croatia. The internal tension was quite considerable; everyone felt that the conflict, a conflict was going to break out, and during that second half of 1991 that the conflict was being prepared and that the instruments were set up with a view to the conflict, with a view to ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, how did the Serbian nationalism manifest itself in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so at the time the first pluralist elections were getting underway, those of December 1990, among other parties, there was a nationalist Serb party that was established, the SDS, that is, the Serb Democratic Party. From the outset its head was Radovan Karadzic. Now, this party, unlike the party in power in Serbia, was not a communist party. It was anti-communist, in fact, and it was supported by the Orthodox Church and the Orthodox Church played an important role in the establishment of this party, the SDS. So this nationalist party, the SDS, had as its official aims to defend the interests of the Serbian people in Bosnia and it got involved in the elections and participated in the coalition that won the elections, but subsequently it participated in the government and in the administration of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Presidency of the Presidency went to the main Bosnian Muslim leader, Alija Izetbegovic. The Presidency of the Council, that is to say, Prime Ministership, went to a Croat and the President of the Assembly went to a member of the SDS, a Serb. Radovan Karadzic did not take on an official position, but remained leader of the SDS party. He also acted as President of the national Serb Council which is a non-official body, but which was supposed to be representing the interests of the Serb people in Bosnia. At the same time, the Serb party, just like the other nationalist parties, made sure that it had power in the opstina, in the municipalities, where it had a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would like to start referring to some of the exhibits that are in your binder. They have not been scanned into the computer, but in your binder there will be the Cyrillic version initially. Then there are French and English translations that follow the Cyrillic versions of these exhibits so you will be able to follow them in your binders.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Bowers, now since you have done with a certain area with Professor Garde, we might see if our fellow Judges have any questions. I just have one question. I am not sure you addressed the matter, but it might be useful: the declaration of independence, did that give rise to any reaction on the part of the international community, and what do you think the significance of those reactions might have been subsequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the declarations of independence as such did not immediately give rise to any reactions on the part of the international community, but in Slovenia and in Croatia when the conflict broke out that gave rise to some reactions, that is to say, there was a war that was being waged. The international community and particularly the European Union could not put an end to it. In Slovenia, it was easy enough precisely because there was no Serb minority in Slovenia, so the Serbs did not see much point in conquering Slovenia. After a few days they had no trouble accepting to withdraw. In Croatia, things were more difficult because the conflict lasted six months. It was bloody. It was dreadful. The efforts of the European Community to put an end to it were initially in vain, and at that point in time some countries, in particular Germany, but other countries as well, thought that the best solution would be to recognise the independence of Slovenia and Croatia, so that the conflict would be officially recognised as an international conflict, and that would allow for outside intervention and intervention by the United Nations that would be legitimate with the view to ending the conflict. Other countries in contrast, for example, France and the UK, thought that it would be best not to recognise the independence of those Republics which would entail recognising the borders. They thought it would be best to wait and to get concessions from those Republics in return for recognising that independence. In particular, what they had in mind was concessions from Croatia in respect of its borders. So there were two opposing ways of viewing the problem. On account of this opposition of views, for six months no decision was taken. During those six months all of the efforts deployed by the international community to put an end to the conflict remained in vain. After six months, finally, that is to say, in December of 1991 the decision was taken to recognise the independence of those Republics. Now, that decision of a condition of recognition was taken on 17th December. The recognition came into effect as of 15th January and Germany jumped the gun -- I do not remember the exact date -- but they went ahead with recognition on their part earlier. At all events, once the recognition did take place it was immediately after that that the fighting in Croatia stopped. They stopped it on 2nd January 1992. You asked me for my opinion, your Honour, it is often said that recognition was premature, that it was one of the causes of the conflict. I read somewhere that that recognition was the actual cause of the war. I think rather the opposite, that the recognition came very late. It was also on account of that recognition that the conflict ended in Croatia. When you say that that is the cause of the war, what you have to know is that that recognition, that decision in December 1991 was taken after some six months of war, rather, there were tens of thousands dead in Croatia. There had already been massacres around Vukovar. There had been dreadful mass murders, mass graves. The war had been lasting for some six months. So to say that it was the recognition that caused the war, it is a bit much because the war had already been going on for six months. Now, recognition, no doubt, did entail recognition of the borders. It crystallised, as it were, the fact that the federation had broken up and, as I said earlier on, this put Bosnia in a very difficult situation. But that is not due to recognition. It is a fact that the federation broke up and I explained the reasons for the breakup earlier on, so it is not by refusing to recognise that breakup by going on and have the federation exist as a fiction when it did not have any further basis in reality that one could have improved things. That is my opinion at all events.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask fellow Judges whether they have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor, earlier on you said that the Yugoslav Army when it attacked Croatia had the support of the militia. Did the militia report to the army? What was their status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the militia was not under the orders of the army. There were two things that were involved, in fact. There were the local militia, that was made up of the local population of Croatia who played a role in the initial events, the roadblocks, etc. and the initial clashes, but there were also paramilitary groups that came from Serbia which had been recruited by some Serbian extremists, extremists, the Arkan Tigers, the White Eagles, and other groupings recruited in Serbia who came and got involved in these operations in Croatia and played a very active role indeed. But, it can be said that even if officially the two types of militia were not under the army's orders, in actual fact, they operated in a co-ordinated fashion, that is to say, that initially the militia, particularly the local militia, would provoke a conflict with the Croats and then, in the second stage, the army would intervene, that is to say, in actual fact it would occupy territory and see to it that there was no possibility for the Croats to reoccupy that territory. Then later on when war really got going as of July/August 1991, then the army attacked such and such a position with shelling and then would occupy the territory, drive out the Croats and then the militia, in particular the militia from Serbia, would come afterwards and proceed with the massacres, pillage etc.. So there were two distinct forces, in fact, three distinction forces, but they acted during this whole period in close co-operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A question I have had on my mind since yesterday when you talked about ethnic cleansing: you said that ethnic cleansing existed since the time of the Austrian Empire; also that it took place during the Nazi period. Could you maybe tell us really when that policy initiated in the former Yugoslavia and where it came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what happened, for instance, in the 18th century under Austrian rule and in the 19th century in Serbian and Montenegrin territory, the Muslims were driven out. Subsequently, what happened then in Croatia and Bosnia in 1941 for the first time it was ethnic cleansing that was practised by representatives of a Christian people on another Christian people, that is to say, by Croats on Serbs. So that was the first time that ethnic cleansing was taking place without for once the Muslims being the victims. That was also the first time where the proportions were as vast, as systematic, as they were. Of course, this was in tune with the fascist Nazi ideology at the time. It is fair to say that ethnic cleansing, such as practised in Croatia during the second half of 1991 and then in Bosnia from 1992 to 1995, that that was also a follow-up to the same kind of operation. But this time it was carried out in a more systematic fashion and a better organised fashion than had ever seen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who practised in the ethnic cleansing by the Serbs this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs against the Croats and against the Croats in Croatia, and I am talking about Croats and non-Serbs, that included the Hungarians who were also victims and in Bosnia it was practised against Croats and, essentially, against the Muslim Bosnians who were in terms of number the main victims. This does not preclude the fact that in Bosnia you also had ethnic cleansing practised by Croats against Bosnian Muslims and vice versa in 1993. But in terms of numbers or statistics, if you like, ethnic cleansing was practised, essentially, by the Serbs. In the course of the 90s, the Serbs took that initiative. They practised ethnic cleansing in a systematic manner. So, from a statistical point of view, it was in very large, considerable numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, if you please, I have just one question in the wake of my fellow Judge's question. How do you define "ethnic cleansing" in terms of its principle and in terms of its method? Then I would have a question on the army, please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, ethnic cleansing is a practice which means that you act in such a way that in a given territory the members of a given ethnic group are eliminated. It means a practice that aims at such and such a territory be, as they meant, ethnically pure. So, in other words, that that territory would no longer contain only members of the ethnic group that took the initiative of cleansing the territory. So, in other words, the members of the other groups are eliminated by different ways, by different methods. You have massacres. Everybody is not massacred, but I mean in terms of numbers, you have massacres in order to scare these populations. Sometimes these massacres are selective, and they aim at eliminating the elite of a given population, but they are massacres. I mean, that is the point. So whenever you have massacres, naturally the other people are driven away. They are afraid. They try to run away and you find yourself with a high number of a given people that have been massacred, persecuted and, of course, in the end these people simply want to leave. They also submitted to such pressures that they go away. They are driven away either on their own initiative or they are deported. But the basic point is for them to be out of that territory and some of them are sometimes locked up in camps. Some women are raped and, furthermore, often times what you have is the destruction of the monuments which marked the presence of a given population in a given territory, for instance, religious places, Catholic churches or mosques are destroyed. So, basically, this is how ethnic cleansing is practised in the course of this war. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: In this connection of ethnic cleansing, Professor Garde, when you speak of "Muslims" are you talking about a religious or an ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. When I talk about Muslims, when I told you about the 18th and 19th century, of course, I was dealing with a religious group, but now when we talk about the Muslims in the course of the 20th century and, more specifically, in Bosnia, we no longer deal with a religious group. As I indicated yesterday, in these particular regions and, more specifically, in Bosnia where the different populations all speak the same language, the difference was based on a confessional criteria, i.e. belonging to a given confessional group. Croats are those that by tradition were Catholics. The Serbs by tradition are orthodox. The Muslim Bosnians are Muslims with a capital "M" belong to the muslim tradition, Muslim this time time spelt with a low case "m". That does not mean that these people had a personal faith in that religion, that they practised that religion. It simply means that by tradition they came from families that are Muslim, that their ancestors also belonged to the Muslim community, but it does not mean at all that they themselves practised the Islam religion or that they believed in what Muslims believe in. The same applies to the Catholics or the orthodox. It simply means that these people belong to that particular community by tradition and they considered a sort of heritage in belonging to that community, and by the other people they were considered as belonging to that community too. But it did not imply anything in terms of their personal creed or their religious practice. Of course, even among the Serbs and even those that claimed that they belonged to the orthodoxy, and though they defended the Orthodox Church, still there are many Serbs that are agnostic or did not believe or anything with no creed. The same applied to Croats and to Muslims, spelt with a capital "M". So again it is not a question of personal faith or creed. It is more a question of belonging to a given group, to a given nation. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If you please, Professor, in your presentation about ethnic cleansing you have referred to deportation and massacre and you also alluded to rape. Can rape be used as a weapon for ethnic cleansing purposes? Has it been used as a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it has. It was used for that purpose because, you know, rape, rape is humiliation, humiliation felt by the woman who is raped and by her whole family and the whole group to which she belongs. Rape is something that makes it even more difficult, even more intolerable, to live together amongst the different groups. Returning in the region where rape takes place, it is even more difficult. So, undoubtedly, that weapon has been used systematically. This being said, in answer to your question, there are certainly better placed experts than me, so I am only repeating here what has been written on this subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You used the word "systematic" when referring to ethnic cleansing. Who promoted this idea or this policy at the beginning in the present conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the present conflict, I mean, this had already been promoted by Serb theoricians before. I mean, there was a text dating back to '37 that clearly explained how we should do away with the Albanians from Kosovo. There were orders given by General Mihajlovic in the Second World War that indicated we need to proceed to ethnic cleansing, probably apocryphal orders but that probably emanated anyway from these Chetnik circles. But the point is that the whole idea was floating in the air and this practise had already existed. So in the present conflict, it is difficult to find or, at least, I for one do not know of any text in which it was expressively said that such populations had to be deported. But, however, it is said expressis verbis everywhere that "we cannot live together any more, we must not live together any more. We must not live with the Muslims under the same roofs". The same idea was found, well, I do not have the text in mind, but anyway, I mean, this whole idea had been expressed before and repeatedly and quite frequently. So the practice was extremely systematic and so clearly enough the idea was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am not sure that we fully addressed the role of the army at the beginning in the federal structure and then gradually the role of the army that developed. Could you briefly give us some clarification about the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. The army was basically the only federal institution that survived. Gradually, at the time when authority was given to the Republics and when the federal Presidency disappeared, all that was left was one single federation institution, i.e. the army. The army has several characteristics. On the one hand, the Serbs for historical reasons, from the origin, the Serbs had always occupied dominating positions. I think there were about 60 per cent of Serb officers while the Serbs only represented 36 per cent of the population in Yugoslavia. If you include the Montenegrins, it increases the proportion. So the Serbs had the dominating positions or posts in the army, and then the army was an institution, a federal institution, as I indicated, but lived on the federation, on the communist regimes since in any communist regime the military were privileged. So the army, the army as a whole, wanted to maintain the federation and, as far as most of the officers are concerned, they wanted to maintain the federation which was directly connected with defending the Serb people. You have General Kadijevic who was the Commander-in-Chief of the army during the crucial times all the way until January '92 who wrote that, when you read him actually you realise that, as far as he was concerned, both objectives were merging into one single objective, i.e. defending the federal institutions and defending the Serbs or defending the rights of the Serbs against all the other peoples. So, when the federal authority disappeared, and it disappeared when the federal Presidency no longer operated on 15th May '91, so at that given point in time you find yourself in front of this rather strange position where you have an army without any Commander, an army that becomes fairly autonomous. So, thanks to the European mediation in July '91, Europe managed to impose the elections of Mesic who is a Croat as a President of the federation. So, theoretically, he was the Commander-in-Chief of the army, but the army never obeyed to him. Mesic, although theoretically the Commander-in-Chief of the army was considered by that army as its No. 1 enemy. So the army did not have any Commander-in-Chief, no superior authority. So the army behaved as an autonomous body and that autonomous body sided with the Serbs and acted in close co-operation with the Serb authorities, that of Milosevic. At that time a Party was created, a Party for Yugoslavia, a Party whose leadership was by Milosevic's wife, Mrs. Markovic, and a few of the commanders of the army. So you see that from that time on the army operates in full autonomy but in close co-operation with the Serb authority.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecutor, now how do you want to organise the rest of the day? I think that this morning we started earlier on, we are going to work until 1 o'clock, we are going to take a break, and you also have some exhibits to tender, so what do you suggest, Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think going through these additional documents should take half an hour to 45 minutes possibly. If it is appropriate, we would like to just continue depending on the staff and the court's wishes. We can take a break, your Honour, if this is an appropriate point.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right. I hope everybody will be agreeable, but we are going to continue with this witness until the end and then we will take a break. Then we will hear the second testimony. So Prosecutor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor Garde and your Honours, if you could turn to Exhibit 4, please? Professor Garde, would you explain to the court what Exhibit 4 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit No. 4 is a letter sent by Radovan Karadzic to Slobodan Milosevic to congratulate him on his election as a President of the Republic of Serbia. There is no date on this exhibit but I probably think that it dates back to December '90 because this is exactly when the election took place, and which are the basis for these congratulations. The interesting thing in this letter is the signature; the fact that Radovan Karadzic signs as the President of the SDS, and at the same time as the President of the national Serb Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is an informal, non-constitutional body which was supposed to represent the interests of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, clearly, here it shows on this exhibit, because of the signature and because of the fact that he congratulates the President of Serbia, he appears as the leader of the Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could move to Exhibit 5, please, if you could explain that exhibit for the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, now, Exhibit No. 5 dates August '91. It is a circular sent by Karadzic as the President of SDS and it is sent to all committees, regional committees and municipal committees, of SDS in Bosnia. This document indicates how the communications should be organised between the different bodies of SDS, and how they would ensure the confidentiality of such communications. So you see here even at the time in August '91 and at the time the war was raging in Croatia, but had not started in Bosnia yet, so these were the preparations for not a clandestine action but a secret or military action and to protect and secure communications of the party without being intercepted by the official authorities in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, if you could move to Exhibit 6, please, and also explain to the court what that Exhibit is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK, Exhibit No. 6 dates back to March '92. It is sent to the President of the municipality and those that are Serb, since it dates back to March 92, the Serb territories or territories considered as being Serb, contrary to the previous period, had been split up into separate territories. So here Radovan Karadzic signs as the President of SDS. He no longer writes to the committees of the SDS, as in the previous exhibit, he is sending this to the Presidents of the municipalities, those municipalities that were placed under his authority at the time when this country had already been split up. So here again the point is to organise communications between the different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, would you move to Exhibit 7, please, and explain that Exhibit to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit 7 is a decision, it is a decision in order to maintain the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the common state of Yugoslavia. The interesting thing is, well, No. 1, this exhibit is not signed by Karadzic but by Krajisnik, Krajisnik who -- in actual fact, I think the interesting thing would be to look at the previous exhibit which is on the same photocopy. It is a decision aiming at creating an assembly of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina; a decision of the same date of 24th October '91. So on 24th October '91 it was decided in a first stage, and that is the first exhibit, the one before, the one about which you are asking me questions. So in this previous exhibit, the decision is made to create a National Assembly or, rather, an Assembly of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a sort of higher degree as opposed to the Council that previously existed. So now you have an Assembly which is supposed to rule over the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So from now on, the Serb people or the Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer recognised the authority of the government of Bosnia Herzegovina, the common government, but they set themselves up as a separate entity. That Assembly of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina is made up of the deputies from SDS and SPO which is another Serb party which were part of the Assembly. So it is a part of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a section of the Assembly, representing these two Serb parties that set themselves up as a separate body. This is why the President of that Assembly is the man, a member of SDS, who previously was a President of the whole Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Momcilo Krajisnik, and this is why he signs that particular exhibit. So, in the first stage, that Assembly is created. This is the first exhibit. Then the second exhibit, No. 7, means that the Assembly which has just been created on that very day decides that the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina will stay in the common state of Yugoslavia. The interesting point is that mention is made that the people will stay part of the common state of Yugoslavia. So, they do not state expressively that it is a member of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia that existed at the time and no mention is made of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which will be created only a couple of months later; they are simply using a word or wording that does not have any constitutional meaning, the common state of Yugoslavia. That means that whatever the form that the state of Yugoslavia will take, the Serbs intend to stay within that state. So it means, it is an act that means that they want to secede secession as from the state of Bosnia. Now, one could wonder why this act is dated 24th October '91. Obviously, this had been prepared for a long time, since before that. You had the autonomous regions, the Serb autonomous regions, so everything had been planned for that particular secession, but what triggered it is the vote that took place on 14th or, rather, 15th October '91, a week before the vote in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina that voted for the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina; a vote that was won thanks to the votes of the Croat and Muslim Bosnians' votes but which was rejected, violently rejected, by the Serb representatives. In the course of that particular hearing of 15th October '91 in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is when Radovan Karadzic voiced very threatening words concerning what could happen if that vote took place. If you please, I am going it read out what he said at the time. I apologise, but I am going to read this out in English because I do not have the Serb origin nor a French translation; what I have here before me is an English translation published in the book of Laura Silber, "The Death of Yugoslavia" on page 237. So Karadzic said before the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "You want to take Bosnia-Herzegovina down the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia are travelling. Do nothing that you will not lead Bosnia into hell, and do nothing that you will not, perhaps, lead the Muslim people into an annihilation because the Muslims cannot defend themselves if there is war. How will you prevent everyone from being killed in Bosnia?" So that is what Karadzic said on 14th and 15th October 1991. This exhibit, Exhibit 7, is, as it were, the implementation of that policy. It is the first step of it, that is to say, the determination on the part of the Serbs to secede from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, both the creation of the Assembly and the affirmation of the Serbian people remaining in whatever Yugoslavia turns out to be, appears on this document known as a gazette. Would you explain to the court what this publication is and its significance, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, the publication, the organ in which that is published, this text?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is published -- it is the official gazette, as it were, of the Serb people in Bosnia Herzegovina. So, the fact that the Serb people publish an official gazette, that is one of the acts in the course of this process of secession, that is to say, the Serb people have set themselves up as a separate entity and they have their own official gazette. But it is worth pointing out that it did not start coming out officially until 15th January 1992, so a bit later. What I was just referring to, 24th October 1991, they were subsequently two or three months later brought together and then published; because in the text itself, in the decision, it says that this decision, this is Article 3, shall be published in the gazette of the people, Serb people, Glasnik. This is a paper that still comes out today. It is a weekly, I believe. It is a normal newspaper. So, initially, once a decision is taken, it is decided that it would be published in the press. Then, subsequently, later on they thought that it would be appropriate to publish it as an official gazette. So a couple of months later they came out with an official gazette and they included all the previous decisions in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Garde. Could we now move to Exhibit 8, please? If you could explain what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 8, this is a decision giving authority to represent and defend the interests of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, in this exhibit there are five people who are given full powers, who are empowered by the Assembly of the Serb people that has just been set up, because all of this is happening on one and the same day, 24th October, so the Assembly gives full agency to five people to represent it on such and such affairs. So it is worth looking more closely at how the responsibility is broken down, because there are two people who are in charge of international affairs, Nikola Koljevic and another person, the two representatives of the Serbs to the Bosnian Presidency. Then there are three other people who are in charge of relations with the federal authorities of Yugoslavia. Now as the previous decision was based on the Serb aim of staying in the common Yugoslav state, so the relations with the federal Yugoslav authorities were what was most important, actually in terms of the functions of the stay of the people that are going to be working in that capacity; Najdanovic who is in charge of relations with the Assembly, the legislative branch; Miodrag Simovic is in charge of relations with the government, federal government: and Radovan Karadzic is in charge of relations with the federal Presidency. That is to say, he is in charge of relations with the supreme authority of the federation. So at this stage, where the aim of the Serbs in Bosnia is to remain within the Yugoslav federation, Karadzic is in charge of the functions which at that point in time are the most important, that is to say, links with the federal Presidency. He cannot be made a member of the federal Presidency officially, but he is in charge of the relations with it, which is just about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move to Exhibit 9, please? If you could explain what that document is and its significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 9 is a decision on the territories of the municipalities of the local communities and places in Bosnia and Herzegovina which regard themselves as part of the federal state of Yugoslavia. So it is still an ambiguous wording there, the federal state of Yugoslavia. Now, secession on the part of the Serb entity was pronounced in the previous decisions. Here, this is a month later, this is 21st November we are talking about, so secession was proclaimed in principle, but the territory has not been specified. So here it is a matter of specifying what that territory is. It is specified as being the territory in which, when the plebiscite was held a little earlier in November -- one second here -- yes, in the course of the plebiscites, more than 50 per cent of the citizens of Serb nationality came out in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia. So, all of these regions where there is more than 50 per cent of the Serb citizens came out in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia are regarded as part of Yugoslavia. So, quite clearly, that is a very elastic definition, because that referendum had been organised throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina and throughout there the majority of Serbs had come out in favour of staying within Yugoslavia. So, I said this was a very elastic formulation that allowed for all kinds of conclusions. There is something else here worth mentioning. It says at the end of Article 4 that the Serbs cannot oppose the decisions taken by the Croats and the Muslims to set up their own entities, which is something totally arbitrary because at that time the Croat and Muslim people had not indicated they wanted to set up their own entities. There had simply been a decision taken by a majority of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly which was mean to represent all of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So there was no desire to secede that had been expressed by the Croat or Muslim communities. In fact, at that point in time, they did not and were not meant to have any separate existence which was quite different from what the Serbs were doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we move to Exhibit 10 now, please, if you could explain the significance of that Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit 10, 21st November '91 still, this is a decision on verifying the autonomous Serb territory proclaimed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a further step, another act, down the road to secession of the Serb territory. It is again a matter of defining that territory. Before the acts we have mentioned here, there had been the setup by the Serbs, by the SDS, of autonomous Serb regions and autonomous Serb districts. That is to say, certain regions had set themselves up as autonomous territories. In other words, they had subtracted themselves from the authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here you have a list of the communities in question. So, it is a matter of delineating the territory of the various regions involved. So, there is one that is somewhat bigger, that is the first one, Krajina, and that is quite widespread. That is why it is called the region, the region of Krajina. Then you have the autonomous districts of eastern Herzegovina, Romanija, Semberija, northern Bosnia. So, this is a list here of the territories that had set themselves up as autonomous Serb territories, and had thereby broken away from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here they are uniting, they are declaring themselves part of Yugoslavia and part of the Serb entity that was being established. So there is this definition of the territory here. It is worth note noting that this decision does not yet lay down any specific borderlines, because the rights, well, since the -- there are some regions, some municipalities where it is indicated that the territory includes only part of it. So, the delineation is not yet as specific as it might be. The previous decision made room for going further, that other territories could be included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, does this creation of the autonomous regions and districts fit into some broader Serbian strategy, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, what is involved here is a longer term strategy, because the aim is to have these territories, which in the first stage have set themselves up as autonomous regions, to have them unite and then they are supposed to unite with Yugoslavia. This is the same process that had been followed in Croatia, because in Croatia as well the Serbs had first set up two autonomous regions. Then those two autonomous regions are joined, united, and the plan was for them to stay within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could have Exhibit 11 which is also R12 shown on the computer screen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not hear the interpretation. There seems to be a problem with the interpretation for the witness. We will straighten that out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now I hear fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Exhibit 11. Professor Garde, would you take a moment and explain to the court what this map represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is Exhibit 11, the map. This is the delineation that we were touching on earlier on, that is to say, this was what was spelled out in the previous act, that is to say, these are all the communities which were supposed to be part of the Serb entity which were going to stay in the common Yugoslav state. So you have the geographical delineation that stems or flows from the previous acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for accuracy and clarification, I would like to make two observations with regard to this map, one is the municipalities of Bosanska Dubica, Bosanski Gradiska and Bosanski Novi are actually not included in a decision that appears in the gazette. We have included them on the map though because, based on our research and investigation, we have the original minutes of the decision actually made by the Assembly. In those minutes, there is an indication that these three municipalities are to be included. So they are included on the map, but I wanted to make that clear to the court. Additionally, the red line that goes through the municipalities of Bosanska Krupa, Gornji Vakuf, Rogatica and Sarajevo are only approximate delineations because the text of the decision, as Professor Garde says, is somewhat flexible and only gives limited guidance on those areas where the territory is only described as including part of that municipality. So those are two clarifications for that particular map. If we could move to Exhibit 12, please, which is R13? Professor Garde, when that comes on the screen, if you could explain that to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map now on the screen is a map showing the military situation on 10th November 1992, that is to say, about a year after the previous map. You can see that it corresponds to a significant extent with the previous map since, roughly speaking, you are talking about the same territories. So, as I said, roughly speaking, it is one and the same territory. So the Serbs occupied militarily something that was very much in line with what they had planned a year earlier. I would point out that there is a mistake here actually on this map, because the Bihac region and these three regions in the north west, in fact, were not occupied by the Serbs at that time. They should not be in red. In fact, they were never taken by the Serbs, so those three north western most regions. But the two maps, I said, are quite close. They do not overlap to 100 per cent, because in some cases the Serbs conquered more territory than they had planned. You can see, for instance, that the whole valley of the Drina to the north east, that is to say, the communities of Visegrad, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Gorazde, all of those regions were conquered by the Serbs but they were not included in what we saw previously. These regions happened to be those where some of the most horrible things took place in connection with ethnic cleansing. There are other areas that were conquered that were not planned for, Jajce, that region, or Brcko to the north, north east -- you can see Brcko which was in white on the previous map and now it is in red, Brcko -- was also the theatre of absolutely dreadful fighting. That was one of the places where ethnic cleansing was carried out in a horrible way. So there are regions where the Serbs met with more resistance than they expected. That is where you have Muslim Bosnian majority, and they had included that in the northern Bosnian region on the previous map, that is, in the north, as you can see here. On this No. 12 around Tuzla, the part going up, that was not planned for on the previous map, that is to say, the Bosnian Muslims put up more resistance than expected. So, in military terms, the situation in November of 1992 was based on what was scheduled a year earlier, but a little bit more territory was taken in some parts and then, of course, there is a little less territory elsewhere and it all very bloody, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Additional clarification on this particular map, your Honours: this line that was drawn was taken from the situation frontline map as developed by the headquarters of the combined British forces of UNPROFOR. In addition to the north western section that Professor Garde mentioned, you may notice that the map does not include the enclaves of Gorazde, Srebrenica and Zepa. It was not until February'93 that those areas started to show up on the situation maps, so that is just a clarification with regard to this particular map. If we could have Exhibit 13, R1-4, just briefly shown? For the court's benefit, this is just the two lines superimposed on each other to show the similarity. I think Professor Garde has already explained the significance of that, so we will move on to Exhibit 14, please. (To the witness): Professor Garde, if you could explain the significance of Exhibit 14 and what the document is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 14 is dated 11th November 1991 -- December 1991. This is an appeal from the Assembly of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina signed by Momcilo Krajisnik, the President. That was calling on the National Yugoslav Army to defend the territories by whatever means, the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as part and parcel of the Yugoslav state, and places where there have been the referendum where the Serbs in a majority had indicated that they wanted to stay in a Serb state. Things had not been spelt out very clearly, but it was now a matter of turning to the Yugoslav Army to have them provide defence. So it is a matter of reiterating the same process that had unfolded in Croatia, that is to say, to have the Yugoslav Army involved in defending the Serb territories as defined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the JNA responded to this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, of course, responded favourably to this request. What happened subsequently went to show that it was the units of the Yugoslav Army which were rebaptised, as it were, to become the Serb Bosnian Army and it was they who were the spearhead of this war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, when you use the term "rebaptised" are you referring to the point in time when the JNA made an official proclamation that it would be withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina; if so, would you explain that and perhaps contrast the so-called withdrawal in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the withdrawals of the JNA in Slovenia and Croatia before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in Slovenia the federal army had accepted to withdraw on the basis of the agreements entered into with the European Community and it did, in fact, withdraw with all its men, its weaponry, its materiel. As far as Croatia goes, the federal army after the cease-fire signed on 2nd January 1992 and the agreement signed subsequently, the federal army withdrew from Croatia and left in the territories of Croatia, they left the forces there but they were rebaptised police forces, but these were the local forces. The federal army did not have to stay there to defend these territories since that task had been taken on by the United Nations. So the federal army did, in fact, withdraw from Croatia, but when it comes to Bosnia, the federal army did not withdraw because what happened was in April and May 1992 the withdrawal was proclaimed but, in fact, all of the units of the federal army, including all their materiel, stayed in Bosnia. Simply what happened was there was a reorganisation of troops so that these units would be made up exclusively, or practically exclusively, of Serbian soldiers from Bosnia so that there was a transfer of men. Soldiers from Bosnia were assigned to units in Bosnia. Those who men who were not from Bosnia were assigned to units in Serbia, Montenegro. Those troops were still called "federal" troops. The troops in Bosnia became the Bosnian-Serb army. So they were meant to be an army of their own, but they kept all their materiel, all their equipment, and they were, in fact, still paid from the federal budget. So while the withdrawal from Slovenia and Croatia did actually take place, when it comes to Bosnia, this was something that was done only theoretically in paper terms. It was just the change of names. That is all that happened and that is why I used the term "rebaptised" earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Garde, if we could move to Exhibit 15 now, please, and explain that particular exhibit to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, Exhibit 15, dated 21st December '91. This is a decision with the aim to creating the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Article 1 you have this strange wording, it says: "Preparation is underway with a view to creating the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina". So, basically, what it means is that Republic is not yet created and the text here provides for preparation with a view to that creation and the Republic should be proclaimed before the new year, the Serb new year, which is 14th January '92. So you see, the time span is rather short. It is about a month or three weeks, rather, which means it is a further step in the constitution of a Serb entity in Bosnia. In the previous text, it was simply indicated that it was to remain part of Yugoslavia, whilst here they decided they are going to make a separate Republic, that of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now one could wonder why that decision was made at the time. Well, that is the time when the European Community has just decided to consider recognising the Republics that would ask for such recognition, a certain time is given for these Republics -- I think it was until 27th December -- to table their application for independence. So, in parallel, the Serbs from Bosnia decide that they could set themselves up in a Republic. They allot themselves a certain time to start this Republic. So again it is the same process of secession and creation of separate entities, which is meant to proceed in parallel with the decisions taken by the other party. So, here it says that such a Republic should be created before 14th January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could move to Exhibit 16, please, and explain that Exhibit to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit 16 is a decision with the aim of creating a Council of Ministers of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the same date, 21st December. So it means that that particular Assembly which had been created previously and which operates as a state, which is going to publish its official journal and which is going to be the basis for a Republic, so before it is actually created we see that the Republic already has a government and that government is described in this Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, one notices that the accused Radovan Karadzic does not appear as one of the ministers in this particular document. Do you have an opinion, could you explain as to why his name would not appear in this formation and selection of the Council of Ministers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is easy to explain. Well, Karadzic is not part of that government because he reserves himself for the function of the President of the Republic. The constitution voted by these Yugoslav Republics all provide for a sort of system based on the 5th Republic of the French system with a clear distinction between the President of the Republic having superior authority and the government, on the other hand. We see that Karadzic is always kept away from the government functions, and we have seen previously that he was in charge of the relationship with the federal authorities, not at the level of the government, but at the level of the Presidency. Here again we see that he is leaving such government positions with other people. He reserves himself for the supreme position which he will occupy later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could move to move to Exhibit 17, please, and if you could explain this Exhibit to the court, taking particular note of Article 1 and Article 2, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This text, we see the constitution given to the so-called Serb Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina. This dates back to -- wait a second -- I am sorry, I am sorry. I think I am a bit confused. This exhibit is a declaration about the proclamation of the Serb Republic of the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, in other words, this is the implementation of the previous act. It was provided for to create a Republic for the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina by 14th January. Now this is 9th January and we see that this Republic is indeed proclaimed. One can see here that in the preamble mention is made of the territorial delineation and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which existed so far. This is what they say. So it means here that for the Bosnian Serbs, this is the act of death of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it existed before. In the future, in Serb media you always refer to the former Bosnia Herzegovina. You have asked me to look at Article 1. Something is the matter with my earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, I think we have overrun the time allotted and I am thinking of a break. I think that we may need to take a short break. I wonder whether on the basis of our agreement we could possibly take a break until quarter to 12 and then we will resume with Professor Garde. His explanations have to be provided to the Tribunal, we do not want to cut him short, but we also have to keep in mind the staff working for this hearing. So, we will stand in recess and we will resume at 11.50. (11.25 a.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (11.50 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor Garde, we were discussing Exhibit 17, in particular Article 1, if you could describe that for the court and explain its significance, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something is the matter with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. We were having problems before the break, I am afraid. I had hoped that the problem had been solved. Is this any better? Can you hear me? Can you hear the Prosecutor? Can you hear the interpreter? This sort of whistling sound has not disappeared, I am afraid. Turning to the technicians, can they do something about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. You were asking me about Article 1 where the territories are defined, territories that are part of the Serb Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mention is made, an interesting mention is made, they talk about autonomous regions and autonomous districts, and the other ethnic Serbian entities in Bosnia Herzegovina which is something extremely vague. Other Serbian ethnic entities, including the including the regions in which the Serbian people remained in minority due to the genocide conducted against it in World War II. So here mention is made of the genocide. I think that that particular wording is extremely vague, so it could be interpreted in any way and could explain any extension of the territory. It is purposeless, since however bloody the genocide might have been against the Serbs in the course of World War II, demographic studies that were carried out later on demonstrated that it did not significantly change the ethnic makeup of the population. It is one of the major Serb myth. According to it, Serbs might have lost the majority in the Bosnia because of that genocide perpetrated between '41 and '45, whilst in actual fact censuses have demonstrated the majority changed not at the time but 30 years later with the first census that shows that the Serbs no longer have the majority which is that of '71. Consequently, it is not true to say that the Serbs lost the majority because of the genocide. I cannot state that in no region there was no change. If you look at the different regions and the different communes, I cannot state, of course, that there was not any change in one particular region or district because of the genocide; and if there were such cases, there were not that many. So this is a wording that really is meaningless, and which will no longer be used in subsequent text. But, anyway, the purpose here is to make that definition as vague as possible, lending itself to any possible extension and, secondly, they refer to a myth which was extremely powerful in the Serb opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, if you could now direct your attention to Article 2 and explain its significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Article 2 says that the Republic, the new Republic, shall remain within the Yugoslav federal state as its federal unit. So once again we talk here about the Yugoslav federal state. So here again this is not an official term which could apply to any form of Yugoslavia and this new Republic is no longer part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it claims to be part of one of the federal units making up Yugoslavia, as was the case for Bosnia-Herzegovina before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move to Exhibit 18 which is a combined set of documents involving the constitution? If you would explain to the court what this Exhibit is and tell them if there is anything significant about the date of the implementation of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, the constitution referred to here is proclaimed on 28th February '92. Why 28th February? Because the 29th, the following day, the referendum was planned, referendum which meant that Bosnia-Herzegovina was to proclaim its independence. So, in the eyes of the Bosnian Serbs at the time when Bosnia-Herzegovina was to proclaim its independence, at that particular time, the new, newly formed Republic that seceded from Bosnia-Herzegovina should have its own constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you direct your attention to Article 2 and explain its significance to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Article 2 is quoting part of the Article that we looked at before as refers to the definition of the territory. So once again reference is made to the territory of the autonomous regions, and the other Serb ethnic entities and then afterwards, it says, including the regions in which genocide was committed against the Serb people in the Second World War. Well, apparently, it repeats exactly the same as in the former Article when in actual fact it is different. Earlier on, we discussed about the regions in which the Serb people found themselves as a minority because of the genocide, whilst here they talk about regions where genocide was committed, which is entirely different. One could think that the authors of that text realised what I said earlier on, which is that the majority had not changed. The demographic majority had not changed because of the genocide. Consequently, the previous text was meaningless. This is my assumption, but the point is that the text here is even more general. There are hardly any regions where the genocide changed the majority. However, the genocide was committed practically everywhere. So when you talk about regions in which genocide was committed, that applies to practically any region in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, as you can see here, the definition of the territory remains extremely imprecise, flexible, lending itself to all sorts of interpretations and conquests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, again in the constitution in Article 3 we have another expression of how this new entity views itself with regard to the federal state or federal entity of Yugoslavia. Would you again review that for the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Article 3 says that the Republic is a part of the federal state of Yugoslavia. It is again the same wording as before. This is again the federal state of Yugoslavia, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, if you could move towards the end of this collective set of documents and look at the constitutional law for implementing the constitution and, in particular, take a look at Article 5 and explain to the court what that Article provides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What number, please? What page, possibly? What exhibit? I cannot find this reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is still Exhibit 18. It will be the last part of the gazette for constitutional -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the constitutional law, that is what you are referring to? OK, yes, I see now. Article 5, it says: "The first President of the Republic shall be elected by the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina under a proposal submitted by at least 20 representatives", and then they talk about 18th November '90. Until then the constitution which we refer to provides for universal suffrage election for the President. Here they say that until the election of the President of the Republic, the function of the President shall be carried out by the members of the Presidency elected previously. These members of the Presidency will be Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic. These two people were to carry out the collective Presidency for that particular time -- at that particular time Radovan Karadzic was not on the forefront and was not the President. His functions were, of course, being the President of the SDS and representing the new Federal Republic within the federal institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Garde, Article 5 provides for, in essence, a general election. To your knowledge, has there ever been this sort of general election for President in the territory that eventually became known as Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wait a second, no, no, no. There was no general election. The general election was provided for by the constitution, but I forgot -- yes, I refer to the second paragraph of Article 5, but I did not refer to the first paragraph of Article 5 in which it says that the President of the Republic shall be elected by the Assembly of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, no such election has ever occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Yes. The election, this general election, never actually took place, but there was an election which is a general election provided for by the constitution itself did not take place. However, there was an election by the Assembly which is covered by the first paragraph in Article 5 of the constitutional law which we are looking at now. That particular election did take place several months later and Radovan Karadzic was elected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Garde. Now if we could move to Exhibit 19, please? Would you explain what this Exhibit is and its significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Exhibit dates from 12th May 1992 and it proclaims the mobilization of the Territorial Defence over the whole territory of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, this is 12th May 1992. For a few weeks now the war has started, the siege of Sarajevo had started, the massacres had started and it is really a matter of legalising the general mobilization of the Serb forces, the local Serb forces, for these operations. It is a matter of mobilizing the Territorial Defence, that is to say, that in the former Yugoslavia you had the army, but you also had this Territorial Defence. The army is already at work and the Territorial Defence is being mobilized as well, which means that there is general mobilization of the Serb people to participate in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could move to Exhibit 20, and again if you would explain its significance to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 20 is -- in fact, there are several amendments here to the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the document we were just looking at. This also dates from 12th May 1992, that is to say, a few weeks after the war actually started and the amendment -- well, the one that is worth mentioning amongst the several amendments is Amendment 3, Article 1.11: "The President of the Republic is henceforth the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces", and that was soon to be Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us move to Exhibit 21 and again explain what Exhibit 21 is and its significance, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 21 is a law, an act, supplementing the constitutional law for implementing the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In it you will find Article 1 there that provides for a new way to appoint, a new way in which the Presidency of the Republic is going to be working. This is the third text really that deals with this matter, because in the constitution of what was planned was universal suffrage. Then in the constitutional law we saw, what was planned was the election by the Assembly. Here there is a third, a provisional way of going about this business on account of circumstances, of course, and here what it says is that the Presidency will be performed by a three-member Presidency elected by the Assembly, and that that Presidency will from within itself choose a President. So, it is a formula similar to what existed in the former Yugoslavia. The Assembly names a Presidency and then the Presidency chooses the President, as it were. So, first, I said there had been talk of universal suffrage, then via the Assembly, and now we have moved up a level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For continuity sake, we will now move instead of to Exhibit 22 to Exhibit 23. We will skip Exhibit 22 and come back to it. Professor Garde, if you could have a look at Exhibit 23 and explain what that particular exhibit does?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well this flows from the previous exhibit. There was to be a Presidency that would be elected and then the President would be elected from them. I said, you have three members in the Presidency, that is, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, who already made up the Presidency before that, who were the Serb representatives to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then we have seen on a previous document that they made up the Presidency of the Serb Republic, but now we are adding Radovan Karadzic here as the third member, but he is mentioned first in the document. So this means that this is the preparatory stage for Radovan Karadzic to become President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, in fact, happens? What does the Presidency do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Presidency, the three-member Presidency, has elected Karadzic as its President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we will move back to Exhibit 22. Professor Garde, if you could explain the significance of Exhibit 22, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 22 has the same date as the previous documents, 12th May 1992, a few weeks after the outbreak of the war. What it provides for is the formation of the army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, the Republic now has an army as of this. What is it that we are talking about? It is made up, in fact, of the units of the federal army which was stationed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In other words, it is a parcel of the federal army that is given a new title on account of the circumstances. Also this army, Article 3, appoints a Commander-in-Chief and that Command-in-Chief is General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then the official proclamation that makes Ratko Mladic the Commander of the main staff of the army and the official proclamation that makes Karadzic the President of the Presidency, the head of the so-called State at that time, those proclamations are on the same date, May 12th 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same day, yes, with the difference, as it were, that in the case of Ratko Mladic, it is a matter of him acceding to that position, whereas as far as Radovan Karadzic goes, even though he formally was not the President of the Republic for quite some time, he had already been the unchallenged leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now if we could move to Exhibit 24, please? Professor Garde, if you could explain what this document is and then again explain the significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 24 is also dated 12th May 1992, like the others. This is a document that dismisses from their function the judiciary. These are people who have been appointed in the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, that these magistrates will be reappointed in the context of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What is really worth mentioning here is that this is the first document which is signed by Radovan Karadzic in his capacity as President of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this is the first document that he signs in that capacity as President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could move to Exhibit 25? Again please explain the significance of this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
