utterances.text: Exhibit 25 is a decision signed also by Radovan Karadzic in his capacity as President of the Presidency of the Republic. It dates 13th May 1992. This document provides for implementing the rules of international law in the army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, to a certain extent what is involved is the fact that Radovan Karadzic has subscribed to the international norms here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now Exhibit 26, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 26 is significantly later, that is from 17th December 1992. This is a decision. It is a proclamation of the election of the President of the Serb Republic, Srpske. The Serb Republic has become the Republika Srpska. This is the proclamation of the election of Radovan Karadzic as President of the Republic. So far he had been the President of the Presidency, that is the third tier I referred to earlier on, and now he is just simply the President elected at a lower level, that is to say, by the Assembly in accordance with one of the documents we looked at earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with regard to Exhibit 26 we will later provide you with the French and English translations. Professor Garde, we have reviewed these various proclamations and decisions as they appear in the official gazette, but setting aside these formal pronouncements, would you just provide your general analysis of what was occurring here for the court's benefit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These documents, despite the formal diversity of the decisions taken, which on the face of it look inconsistent because in one document the elections are going to take place, in another document a different way, people in different offices, etc., but if you look at this chronologically and you look at the logic behind it, these documents would tend to show that Radovan Karadzic was always the key player, the unchallenged leader of the Serbs in Bosnia. Chronologically, you can distinguish three phases. Up until October 1991 officially you have the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina operating with three constituent peoples, and you have a coalition of the three national parties in power. They distributed power amongst themselves, as we have seen. The Muslims had the Presidency, a Croat was in charge of the government and a Serb was in charge of the Presidency of the Assembly. So the Serbs left the executive branch in the hands of the two others, and satisfied themselves with the legislative authority, that is to say, the Presidency of the legislative branch, which is to say that they did not want to get too heavily involved in the workings of that Republic because they are already thinking of breaking away from it. The person they have appointed to act as President of the Assembly, it is not the leader, their leader, the leader of their party, Radovan Karadzic, it is a different character who is not without importance or responsibility, but he was not the boss, as it were, Krajisnik. But Radovan Karadzic holds the key position as leader of the party, that is to say, the leader of one of the three parties in the coalition. He is the leader of the dominant Serb party and at the same time he is in charge of the Serb Council, the National Serb Council, which is the formal body of the Serbs in Bosnia. So up until October 1991, that is to say, up until the Bosnian parliament in that memorable session I referred to earlier on when Karadzic said those threatening words I quoted for you, there is the sovereignty of Bosnia that is adopted and then the plan for succession, for the breaking away of the Serb entity that is already getting under way. During this period the decision is taken by the Serbs that, despite the decision that has been taken by the parliament, their territory, which they start delineating at that point in time will stay part of Yugoslavia as an entity. So what is the main position then? It is the relations with the federal authority, and that is the position that Radovan Karadzic takes on. We saw that in one of the documents we looked at. Later when it comes to the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the secession of the Serb territories to establish a Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when that actually takes place, then Radovan Karadzic has himself elected by various procedures to the office that he set aside for himself from the outset, that is say, the office of President of the Republic. So there is some continuity through these events. They look inconsistent on the face of it, but there is this continuity that is quite logical that runs throughout them and goes to show that at no point in time Radovan Karadzic was not the boss. I would also like to draw your attention to something else. These decisions on the face of it would seem not to have any implications when it comes to the conduct of military operations and ethnic cleansing that start taking place as of March 1992, but what you have to bear in mind is something of quite some significance, that is the Croatian precedent, because the process unfolding here that you can see through these documents is exactly the same process that had been carried out by the Croatian Serbs a few months earlier, roughly speaking a year earlier. That is to say, first the territories with Serb majorities are claiming such, establishing themselves as a separate entity, as an autonomous region, then they unite to form a Republic. It is the Krajina Republic that was set up in Croatia and you have the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina, later on Republika Srpska there. So they established themselves on that basis. They planned to stay in Yugoslavia, and then at the end they go ahead with cleansing their territory, with the ethnic cleansing of their territory, in that very bloody fashion. So the process unfolded in Croatia. It started in Croatia in mid-1990 and the bloody period of ethnic cleansing in Croatia took place in the second half of 1991. So, at the time when the Bosnian Serbs go ahead with the first stages of this process, that is to say in October 1991, it is already known on the basis of the Croatian precedent where it is going to all end up. It is going to end up in a lot of blood and ethnic cleansing. It is exactly the same itinerary that was to be followed a little later by the Bosnian Serbs under the leadership of Radovan Karadzic. With regard to these documents we have pursued, on the face of it they are quite innocent, even though they point to something very serious, that is to say, the delineation of the territory, but they do not say that the delineation of the territory must entail the deportation of the non-Serbs living there. That is not on paper anyway, but we know on the basis of the Croatian precedent that that is how things happened. I would add in regard to ethnic cleansing, that is not a necessary logical consequence to the delineation of the territory. That is to say, you have to set up a Serb state, you have to set up a state dominated by the Serbs, all the Serbs will be there, etc. In logical terms that does not necessarily mean that there should only be Serbs living in that territory. So, conceivably, there could be a greater Serbia or a Serb state that would have been established but which would have tolerated within it the presence of minorities. That is what you have in other Balkan countries. I do not know, take Romania, Bulgaria or even Serbia itself, there are people there who are dominating, but there are also minorities which are tolerated. In addition, in Serbia itself there are people who are in favour of a greater Serbia but who are also in favour of co-existence within that greater Serbia of various peoples. You can think of the Serb leader Vuk Draskovic and his party, the Serb Renewal Movement, which as of the 80s was one of the main exponents of having all the Serbs in one state, in a greater Serbia, but at one and the same time always affirmed that in that state the Serbs should live alongside with the Muslims and the Croats. So, in other words, was always opposed to ethnic cleansing, and little by little went into opposition, even violent opposition, with the other victors of Serbian nationalism as ethnic cleansing went ahead. So a greater Serbia does not necessarily in logical terms mean that there is going to be ethnic cleansing, but the Croatian example went to show that, de facto, that is what it would mean. At the time the Bosnian Serbs started up the process that we have just been running through on the basis of the documents, they already knew that that process would lead to ethnic cleansing, and they also made use of the same people who had been involved in ethnic cleansing in Croatia. So, behind the strictly legal and apparently innocent documents, there is this process that is very logical, that is very methodical and which would lead to ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and which began a few weeks before the last documents we have looked at, since it began, roughly speaking, in March 1992 and the last documents we have reviewed date from May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORROWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Garde. That concludes the questions from the Prosecutor. We would tender all of these exhibits to the Court as evidence for the Rule 61 hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, prosecuting counsel. Fellow judges, Judge Odio Benito, do you have a question? You have the floor, madam. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Professor, I would like to know if you could give us your opinion about the administrative personnel or political links, if any, between Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that at the time we are talking about those links were very close indeed. The whole process which we have surveyed, that is to say, the process of secession on the part of the Serb territories from Bosnia and Herzegovina, their desire to stay part and parcel of Yugoslavia, that was done in close co-operation with the Serb authority. That is proven best by the fact that this division, this nominal division splitting of the army with the assent and the participation of both parties, that is to say the Serb authority of Milosevic and then of the Bosnian Serb authority on the other. So there was this friendly separating of the ways between these two fragments which were in fact closely linked, the fact that the army went on being paid by Belgrade. It is quite clear that at that time there were extremely close links. Subordination was practically entire between the Bosnian Serb authority and Serbian authority. Later on, much later, there were some differences of view and a bit of friction, but at the time we are talking about here, that is to say when the war started, I think the subordination was entire. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor, I understand there was a sort of inconsistency between two documents, No. 20 and No. 22, regarding the Commander-in-Chief of the army in Exhibit 20. According to your translation it says that the President will soon become the chief of the army. This is what you said I think. Then you said that that particular President was Mr. Karadzic. Then later on in Exhibit 22 it states that Mladic is the Commander-in-Chief of the army. So, I wonder whether there is a commander and a chief of the army. The army was under the authority of whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that like in most countries in the world you have a military commander of the army. However, the head of state in its capacity is also the commander of the army. It is the same in France. It is the same in many countries in the world. So in the Serb Republic of Bosnia they applied exactly the same principle. You have a military commander who has to report to the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this case then, in practical terms, in concrete terms, where did the orders come from in this particular instance and according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, well, you know, I am not a military expert, but I suppose that as in many similar cases the general orders come from the Presidency of the Republic, and as far as implementing orders they are taken by the military Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is a sort of hierarchy in the different orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Yes indeed. So the great strategy is designed by the President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if you please, you have demonstrated that this was a logical process in terms of ethnic cleansing and a plan that was implemented in Croatia was also implemented in Bosnia in a systematic manner. Since we are dealing with a strategy here, who was the master mind behind this strategy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that as regards Bosnia the main responsibilities were incumbent upon Karadzic in general terms, but at the same time I believe there was a very close tight team. There were people, well, as far as we can judge of course, there was a unity of view between the main leaders whose names are known and we have seen them before like Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and many others. All these people made up a very close tie, General Mladic of course as well. In general terms, all the operations, and I include here what took place in Bosnia but also what had taken place before in Croatia, I think that one of the master minds, one of the main people, is Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor, we are not going to keep you much longer, longer than is necessary, but before the end of your testimony we have referred to the military role taken by Mr. Radovan Karadzic. According to you, was there a political role played by General Mladic, or was General Mladic only a military subordinate, at a very high level of course, but did he have any political agenda? Was there a political career as regards Mr. Mladic which could explain a certain number of things. I would like to get your view on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the case of General Mladic, I think that he had his own strong political convictions. General Mladic for one before he was the commander in Bosnia was a Commander in Croatia. He in '91 was Commander in Knin in Croatia, in this region where Serbs inhabited that part of Croatia. So General Mladic participated in the first phase of the war and of ethnic cleansing that took place in Croatia in '92, but also participated in the second stage in Bosnia from '92 through '95. So he fulfilled, if you like, the same functions, probably at a lower level of authority in Croatia, still he was commanding. So undoubtedly he -- well, honestly, I do not know whether we can make any difference between a military responsibility and a political responsibility. The two are closely tied.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor, I think the time has come to end your testimony. I have just one last question, if you please. Have you got the feeling that you were able to express your complete view before this Tribunal? I would have liked to ask you if there was something you wanted to add beyond or outside the questions, or something that was not covered by the Prosecutor's questions or our questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I have the feeling I was able to express myself fully. Sometimes some of the questions I am afraid I was not able to completely answer. I think I was in a position to answer some of the questions expressing my own views, but I am afraid I am not sure if I was able to sufficiently answer the questions, but sometimes I had the sufficient documents to support my views.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. We are very grateful for your long testimony, probably very tiring for you. Now that we have completed your testimony we would like to thank you very much. Prosecutor, I think that we can usher out Professor Garde and we could possibly introduce the following witness. Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, it is 10 to 1. We are going to try to stick to our timetable. So we are now going to introduce the following witness and, if you please, we are going to start only with preliminary questions with the witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That will be fine your Honour. Your Honour, before we bring in the next witness we have prepared three binders with exhibits for the convenience of the court, so that it can follow the testimony of Mr. Ralston who will be our next witness. Perhaps they can be sent up to the court. Mr. John Ralston, called. Examined by Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will introduce the next witness in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor. We were just receiving the binder. I think we are ready to listen. We are going to turn to the witness. Can he be given a head set, yes? Can you hear yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Ralston, I think you are now going to take your oath, as is the case for any witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Mr. Ralston starts his testimony, as you are aware the Office of the Prosecutor has been conducting a wide-ranging criminal investigation into the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the course of these investigations we have collected an enormous amount of evidence. Mr. Ralston has been called to testify today to describe some ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston has been called as a summary witness to describe some but not all of the findings of the Office of the Prosecutor. Obviously, this is an immense task in the short amount of time that Mr. Ralston has to testify before this Court. In order to provide the Court with the most comprehensive answers on a wide-ranging examination of subjects, Mr. Ralston has prepared written answers to many of my questions. He will be reading into the record some of his answers to those questions. I would propose, your Honours, that I start the examination of Mr. Ralston by asking him questions about his background and then we break, because I am going to go straight on from there into a fairly large examination of the Serbian Democratic Party. So, if I could start by asking you, Mr. Ralston, to state your name please and spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My full name is John Hunter Ralston, R-A-L-S-T-O-N.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before being employed by the Office of the Prosecutor, where were you employed and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I commenced in employment in 1972 as a Police Officer in Australia. I worked as a Detective with the New South Wales police with the Homicide Squad. I then worked as a Senior Project Officer with the New South Wales Department of Consumer Affairs. Later I worked for the Commonwealth Attorney Generals Department as a senior investigator in that Department's Nazi War Crimes Investigation Unit. Following that I worked with the National Crime Authority in Australia which is the body responsible for investigating organised crime. From that position I came to the Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been employed at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been employed with the Office of the Prosecutor since 16th June 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are your duties and responsibilities at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an Investigations Commander with the Office of the Prosecutor. Initially my duties were to lead an investigation team within the Office, and from November 1995 I have held the position of Investigating Commander. My duties have involved the responsibility for overall co-ordination of investigations in relation to Dr. Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the court wishes me to continue with my examination I am prepared to do so. Otherwise I will leave it to your Honour's discretion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecutor. I think we are going to stand in recess now until 2.30. (1.00 p.m.) (LuncheonAdjournment) (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. The first subject that Mr. Ralston will be testifying about is the Serbian Democratic Party, its structure and evolution. He will also describe for you Dr. Karadzic's role in the party. In the course of my examining Mr. Ralston, I will be referring to the Serbian Democratic Party as the SDS. So, Mr. Ralston, let me turn to you and begin by asking you what is the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS, a political party. As a result of the November 1990 elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina emerged as the dominant political force among the Bosnian Serbs. Of the 240 seats in the two chambers of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly, after the 1990 elections, the SDS won 72 or 30 per cent of the seats, with the most of the rest of the seats going to the Muslim SDA or the Croatian HDZ parties. Only about 15 per cent of the Serbian members of the New Assembly were not members of the SDS (13 in total).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is the SDS important in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS is important because it became the political vehicle through which Karadzic emerged as the paramount leader in the Bosnian Serb administration. Before the conflict started, it was the political entity through which the majority Bosnian Serb political will was exercised, and it remains so today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it established, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS was established at a conference in Sarajevo in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court how it was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, it was formed at a conference (attended by all prospective members). The conference adopted a "democratically inspired" approach, and Karadzic welcomed into the ranks of the SDS all those, including "democratically" oriented members of the League of Communists, who accepted it. The party was organised on the republic, regional, sub-regional, municipal and local commune levels. Committees at the regional level and below were to be autonomous in regard to local political evaluations and personnel decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the SDS active throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The party was established in eight regions, Bosanska Krajina, Central Bosnia, Eastern Bosnia, Eastern Herzegovina, Northern Bosnia, Western Bosnia, South-eastern Bosnia and Western Herzegovina. The regions were divided into sub-regions, municipalities and local areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please identify the leaders of the SDS before the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Leaders of the SDS included Dr. Radovan Karadzic, the President, Aleksa Buha and Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain if the SDS was well organised throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout -- I am sorry, before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our research indicates it was a well organised political body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I think we lost you on the audio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our research indicates it was a well organised political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, would you please refer to Exhibit No. 27 in your binder as well as Exhibit No. 28? I would ask you to identify each of those exhibits and explain the significance to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly, this document dated 15th August 1991 sets out operating instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, prosecuting counsel, these documents have not been translated into French, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have not been, apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would simply like to point out that the presiding Judge happens to be French and I would just point out that French is an official language of our Tribunal. I understand, in so far as possible, the difficulties and we do have a limited number of interpreters and I know that a lot of work has been done on this score. But, as far as the documents go that we received this morning, along with Mr. Garde's documents this morning, they had been translated, but I would just like to remind you that this is one of the official languages of the Tribunal that we are talking about. So I would like this to be recorded in the transcript. I would to ask that, in so far as possible, we abide by this fundamental principle of the Tribunal, that is to say, we have two official languages, English and French. Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We apologise to your Honour for any convenience in not having this document in French, but due to the translators working on the previous documents, we were unable to complete all of the translations. (To the witness): Mr. Ralston, would you please continue with your testimony, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I was pointing out, this document dated 15th August 1991 to all SDS municipal board sets out operating instructions for the municipal boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you also refer to Exhibit No. 28, please, and explain to the court its significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I refer to this document again later in my testimony, but the significance of the document, again it is addressed to all Presidents of the municipalities. It is dated 23rd March 1992. The main effect of this document is setting out how the communications system would operate, and setting out the organisation of communications systems between the various municipalities, the SDS representatives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, let me ask you, what were the goals of the SDS and what was the position the SDS in the event of the SFRY disintegrated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In his report to the founding conference, the party's new President, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, decried what he saw as the unfavourable economic, demographic and political position of the Serbian nation. Recalling the genocide to which the Serbs had been subjected during World War II, he claimed that they had continued genocide against themselves when peace came, destroying their own national and cultural identity by devoting themselves, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to a system which seemed to have been created specifically for the purpose of their national destruction. The important part: under these conditions Dr. Karadzic stated the SDS was being created with its main goal as the complete and unconditional civil, national, cultural, religious and economic equality of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its most important political goal was a federal Yugoslavia and within it a federal Bosnia-Herzegovina. In case this should not be possible, Karadzic said the goal of the SDS would be the enablement of democratic methods as the response of the Serbian people to any new situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, did Dr. Karadzic ever express what would happen if Bosnia declared independence and withdraw from the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did in a public statement to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Around midnight on 14/15th October 1991, he made a speech from the podium during an address regarding moves towards independence by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This address provided an insight into probable SDS reaction to independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, a portion of this was described this morning in the testimony of Professor Garde. We have a film clip of that speech, or a portion of that speech, which we would now like to present to the court, so if we could please play Exhibit No. 29, clip 1?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting counsel -- well, the technician has answered the Judge's question about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. (Exhibit 29 was played) Mr. Ralston, were non-Serbs allowed to join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In theory, yes. According to the party statutes, adopted on 12th July 1990, membership in the party was open to all adult citizens of Serbian nationality as well as members of other nationalities who voluntarily accepted its programmes and statutes. However, it must be noted that the main point of the programme of the SDS at this time was to remain in the SFRY, at a time when it was becoming increasingly unattractive for other nationalities to do so. This was at the time Croatia and Slovenia were well on the road to independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the areas where the Bosnian Serbs did take control, were non-Serbs required to pledge allegiance to the newly formed Bosnian Serb state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the areas where Serbs took control, non-Serbs were asked to sign a pledge of allegiance to the Serbian authorities. Often this was necessary to remain in their former positions. However, as our investigations have shown, this pledge did not allow them to remain in their positions for long. Our research has shown that after a few months they would have been summarily dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, at the time the conflict started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was there any significant participation of non-Serbs in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, judging by the names of these people, all the leading members were either Serbs or Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to turn to a series of questions related to how the SDS was structured. Can you, please, inform the court how the SDS was structured, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1990 Statutes created the following central party organs: the Party Assembly, the Party President, the Main Board, the Executive Board, the Supervisory Board and the Court of Honour. In 1991, these organs were all redesignated as the Assembly etc., of the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Court of Honour was eliminated and a Statutes Council and other Councils of the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina were simultaneously added. Radovan Karadzic was the Party President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the court the purpose and functions of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Assembly was the highest party organ. It was originally to consist of all party members until their number exceeded a thousand, after which the Main Board would devise a principle of representation. The 1991 Draft Statutes supplied such a principle by providing that the assemblies of municipal and city organisations would send representatives, the total number of which was not to exceed 300.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was this Assembly supposed to meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Assembly was to meet once a year. Originally, only more frequent meetings were to take place at the decision of the Main Board, but in 1991 it was stipulated that any decision on convening the Assembly was to be made by the Main Board at the President's proposal. At the same time, the President was obligated to convene the Assembly at the request of at least one third of all the representatives or 15 municipal organisations. The Assembly had to be convened by the President or someone authorised by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the functions of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Assembly was responsible for adopting and amending the party Programme and Statutes. The other functions of the Assembly were of a strictly organisational character. The most important of these were the election and recall of the President and the members of the Main Board, Supervisory Board and Statutes Council. It also had the final say in financial matters, including fixing the amount of dues and the manner of their distribution. The Assembly thus only had an indirect influence on the party's policy and day-to-day operations. It was even empowered to transfer part of its business to the President or the Main Board. The Assembly which convened in July 1991 was the second and last SDS Assembly before the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, you mentioned earlier that the SDS created party Presidency and that Dr. Karadzic was its President. What was his role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The President, Karadzic, represented the SDS. He could also designate someone else to perform this function, although the 1991 Draft Statutes specified that this must be a member of the Main Board. The President was in addition ex-officio chairman of the Main Board. The term of office was originally set at two years but later extended to four, with the right of re-election in either case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were his responsibilities as the President of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His responsibilities, or his most important responsibilities, were to co-ordinate the work of the party organs, to see to the realisation of the programmatic tasks and goals of the party and to represent the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were his duties as President of the SDS ever expanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991 this list of rights was expanded to include making political and other decisions in the name of the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina in so far as they are not within the competence of other organs and bodies of the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina, and performing other matters which the Assembly of the SDS or the Main Board of the SDS places within his competence and having, in extraordinary situations within society, extraordinary powers within the competence of the Assembly and the Main Board. The President was responsible for his work to the membership, to the Assembly and to the Main Board of the SDS. His powers were accordingly considerable. They were susceptible of such broad extension in "extraordinary situations" as to be practically open-ended, and in normal times they were limited only to the accession of authority in "other matters". The President had more than enough scope for initiative and independent action to make him far and away the leading figure in the party. His actual power was thus likely to be a function of his only personality and standing within the organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, did Dr. Karadzic insist on strong central control of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. The need for their actions to be well planned and controlled is apparent from his address to the Presidents of the SDS controlled municipalities in a speech in November 1991 during the campaign for the "Plebiscite of the Serbian People".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a transcript of that speech, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to refer you to Exhibit No. 30 in the binders. Mr. Ralston, could you please read from that exhibit relevant portions of the speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a lengthy document, but I will go to a paragraph towards the end, part of the penultimate paragraph on page 10. In his speech, among others things, Dr. Karadzic said: "I am asking you to be energetic and strict; to get ready and establish your authority in your territories; in municipalities; regions, local communities, and to prepare yourselves for restructuring and regionalising the municipalities. But I am begging you here, that you should in no situation think that someone else has to do the job and that you leave a job unfinished, but to control it to the very last moment. To control it to the very end, not to be sloppy and careless".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you also please to refer to Exhibit No. 28? Can you identify that document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Exhibit I spoke about previously. It is a document addressed to the Presidents of the municipalities dated 23rd March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature appears on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read to the court the relevant portions of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I will start midway, I will start with the second paragraph of the document: "Taking into consideration that one of the essential conditions for the protection of Serbian people in the situation that has been created requires rapid and timely transfer of data and information relevant to defence and security, as well as transfer of decisions, directions and instructions by the government bodies. We have established a Republic operation centre and decided that, in addition to the regional centre in Banja Luka, the municipal centres take over the function of regional centres; Sekovici for the autonomous region of Bihac; Trebinje for the autonomous region of East Herzegovina; Sokolac for Autonomous Region Romanija; Bijeljina, Autonomous Region Semberija; also, a municipal centre ought to be formed in the municipality of Petrovo which would take over the function of the regional centre for the Autonomous Region North Bosnia. Regional centres in Banja Luka, Trebinje, Sokolac and Bijeljina are already connected with the Republic centre of TT", I am advised that that means telegraph and telephone, "and radio communications, while the regional centres of Sekovici and Petrovo will be connected until March 26th 1992". Taking that a bit further, the municipalities now face an obligation to urgently connect their own information centres with the regional centres, if it has not been done so far, and provide for the personnel and other requirements in order to monitor the situation in the field. Keeping in mind the current situation of the Republic, it is necessary to co-operate with the SJB, which is the Public Security Service, by providing the centres with a duty shift and ability to convey and receive information 24 hours a day non-stop Saturdays and Sundays". Later in the same document he says: "With regard to the above, it would be useful if you personally inform yourself on the state -- in the information centres in your municipality as well as on their performance capability".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the significance of that document, in your opinion, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance of that document, in my opinion, is it shows planning, it shows co-ordination and provision for information to flow both up and down from the highest levels of the SDS to the lowest levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Ralston, now let me turn to the Main Board. You have testified earlier that the SDS also established a Main Board. Could you please tell the court what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Main Board was the highest organ of the party between sessions of the Assembly. It was originally to have 57 members, including at least two from each of the regions and one from each sub-region and members were to be elected for two years with the right of re-election. However, in 1991 the size was reduced to 45 members, elected from among the Assembly's representatives with account being taken of territorial representation. The term was increased to four years with one third of members being eligible for re-election.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the functions of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the 1990 Statutes, the Main Board had numerous functions, including the following: electing the members of the Executive Board of the Party; preparing drafts of all acts and decisions which the Assembly adopts; adopting decisions which the Assembly gives its authorisation for; seeing to the correct execution of the Assembly decisions; electing members of temporary or provisional Party bodies and preparing the electoral programme of the Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those functions ever expanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991 the Main Board was entrusted with "especially handling" several matters including electing the chairman and two thirds of the members of the Executive Board of the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina; preparing drafts of all acts, documents and decisions which the Assembly of the SDS adopted; deciding on the territorial organisation of the SDS; electing temporary and permanent working bodies and commissions and establishing their competence; executing decisions of the Assembly of the SDS; examining and adopting reports on the work of the municipal and city boards; setting out guidelines and adopting decisions for the work of the municipality and, as necessary, the local boards of the SDS; to examine, as necessary, reports on the work of organs and bodies of the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, now I would like to turn your attention to another component of the SDS, that is, the SDS Crisis Staff. Can you please explain to the court what they were and what was their significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was an organ which was supposed to be established on all levels of society in the SFRY in times of war or other serious emergency in order to coordinate the security activities on that level of society. The SDS established Serbian-controlled crisis staffs outside the jurisdiction of the legitimate republic, municipal and local commune authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This dramatically reduced the control of legitimate republic authorities in Sarajevo, and significantly contributed to the effective abolishment of legitimate government control altogether in a high number of municipalities with a Serbian demographic and political majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the SDS establish Crisis Staffs in the areas that were taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Crisis Staffs were more or less established openly several months before the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the headquarters of the SDS and in municipalities with Bosnian-Serb political majority and control. In Bosnian municipalities with a non-Serbian majority, Crisis Staffs were normally established underground by the SDS long before the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina started, and when the Bosnian Serbs took power in such municipalities the Crisis Staff surfaced as the supreme co-ordinating organ of the municipality. This happened, for example, in Prijedor on 30th April 1992 and Kotor Varos on 11th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, please, provide to the court some examples of how the SDS operated in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will provide examples from Foca and Prijedor. In Foca, when the new national parties were formed, both the SDA, the predominantly Muslim party, and the SDS held large rallies. The SDA rally was held in August 1990 with the SDS rally coming two weeks later in September 1990. Several persons who would later become key personnel in the Bosnian Serb leadership attended the SDS rally. Dr. Radovan Karadzic and Biljana Plavsic both attended, along with Vojislav Maksimovic, Velibor Ostojic, Miro Stanic and Peko Cancar. Maksimovic had been a teacher in Foca, later he became a professor of literature at the University of Sarajevo, before becoming the first president of the SDS Club of Deputies in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly. Velibor Ostojic, the current Minister of Education and Information of "Republika Srpska" and the President of the Executive Board of the SDS, was formerly Minister of Information and an SDS Deputy from Foca. Before the war he worked at the Sarajevo radio and television station. Peko Cancar, a local attorney, was also in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the local SDS's role in the Foca Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the local Municipal Assembly in Foca, the SDS held about 30 seats of a total of 70. Prior to the takeover, the Serb members of the local Assembly started boycotting assembly meetings in order to delay decisions that had to be made on the municipal level. Soon thereafter, the SDS started to separate from all aspects of municipal life and establish their own institutions. Simultaneously, the Serbs started to arm themselves with the support of the JNA. After the parties were formed in 1990, Ostojic and Maksimovic moved to Sarajevo, while Cancar remained in Foca. As leading members of the SDS, all three visited Foca several times to organise meetings and make speeches. In the beginning of April 1992, the three men reportedly established a Serbian Crisis Staff and a Serbian Police Force. The head of the Crisis Staff, Miro Stanisic, was the President of the SDS in Foca. Following the takeover, Karadzic was seen meeting with representatives of the Serbian Crisis Staff. On 6th April 1992, Ostojic and Maksimovic reportedly held a meeting of the SDS staff in the Orthodox Church in Foca; a meeting which was also attended by a group of JNA officers. After that meeting, an ultimatum was issued to the SDA district committee representatives for the entire Muslim population of Foca to hand over their weapons, gather under the escort of the Serbian army and police and leave town. After the takeover, Maksimovic and Ostojic were responsible for arming the Serbian population in and around Foca, holding meetings were local Serbian leaders and organising military training for volunteers. Speeches by Maksimovic and Ostojic were broadcast on the local radio station. Coincidentally, a weeks before the attack on Foca, one witness read a letter by Ostojic addressed to the SDS, entitled: "What to do in case of war". The letter stated that the radio station and then the police station should be taken over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the SDS operate in Prijedor, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 1990 elections in Prijedor, the Muslim SDA won a plurality of seats in the Prijedor municipal assembly. Nevertheless, during the succeeding months, Bosnian Serb officials who had previously dominated key positions in the municipality, resisted a reallocation of power consistent with the electoral results. In the spring of 1991, Serbian politicians in Banja Luka, the regional centre approximately 45 kilometres from Prijedor, proclaimed a separate Serbian regional community of municipalities which was transformed into the autonomous region of Krajina in September 1991. The municipalities in north western Bosnia, with the exception of Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kotor Varos, gradually decided to join the community. Late in 1991, Serbs in Prijedor and elsewhere in Bosnia were directed by the central SDS leadership to assemble a shadow government. Local Bosnian Serbs leaders were instructed to ensure their ability to control all levels of municipal life, including police, finance and communications and to ensure co-operation with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the Bosnian Serbs seize power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 30th April 1992, the Serbs seized power in Prijedor and the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor became the supreme power in the municipality. The Crisis Staff was made up of persons from the military, the police, as well as the civil administration. The most powerful positions in the Crisis Staff were held by the SDS leadership, the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify some of those members of the Prijedor SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Simo Miskovic was President of the SDS and head of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. He was seen by a number of witnesses in the detention camp, Omarska and Keraterm, during their operations. Colonel (now General) Vladimir Arsic, a JNA officer before the conflict in Prijedor, was appointed commander of the Prijedor barracks. Major Radmilo Zeljaja became the field commander for Colonel Arsic and led many of the operations relating to ethnic cleansing in the villages. Zeljaja directed the attack against Kozarac, participating in negotiations leading up to the attack and played a leading role in the surrender of civilians from that town. The name of the town of Kozarac was later changed to Radmilovo, in honour of Zeljaja's conquest. Later, Zeljaja visited the Omarska came with a delegation of Serbs from Banja Luka and Prijedor in July 1992. Major Slobodan Kuruzovic, a former school teacher, was a member of the Crisis Staff and the Commander of the Trnopolje camp. He also took part in rounding up of civilians living in villages on the left bank of the Sana River in July 1992. Simo Drljaca, another significant figure, became the Chief of Police of the Prijedor municipality after the takeover. Following the takeover and arrest and detention of thousands of non-Serbs -- sorry, became the Chief of Police following the takeover and arrest and detention of thousands of non-Serb civilians. Drljaca played a key role in the administration of the detention camps and was repeatedly seen in all three detention camps in the area, Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje. Since co-ordinating the takeover of Prijedor, Drljaca was promoted to Deputy Minister of Interior of the Bosnian Serb Republic. Dr. Milomir Stakic unlawfully replaced Muhamed Cehajic as the President of the municipality Prijedor after the take-over by Serbian forces on 30th April 1992. In interviews with the media, Stakic acknowledged the existence of the camps at Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje. A number of persons saw Stakic visiting these camps during their operations. Srdo Srdic was an SDS Deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later in the "Republika Srpska" Assembly. He was also seen in the Omarska and Keraterm camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Ralston will now testify about the Bosnian Serb administration and describe Dr. Karadzic's role and authority in it. (To the witness): Mr. Ralston, when did the Bosnian Serb administration come into existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb entity has gone through different phases in its evolution, culminating with the establishment of Republika Srpska. Already on 21st December 1991, the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina decided conditionally to establish the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina before 14th January 1992. On 9th January 1992, that Assembly adopted a declaration on the proclamation of the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The 28th February 1992 constitution adopted by the same Assembly referred to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and stated in its Article 3 that the entity was "a part of the federal state of Yugoslavia". The constitution entered into force on day of its adoption according to its own implementation legislation. Key legislation on government, defence and internal affairs was also adopted on 28th February 1992. So by that date the foundation of the Bosnian Serb legal infrastructure was in place, and during the following two to three months the central administration entity was set up. Vice Presidents, Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic functioned as President of the entity between 28th February and the time Karadzic became President. On 12th August 1992 the entity change its name to "Republika Srpska" or "the Republic of Srpska" which it has gradually become known as.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, has the investigation shown any relationship between the leadership of the SDS and the leadership of the Bosnian Serb administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please refer to Exhibit No. 31 and explain the significance of Exhibit 31 to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you look at this Exhibit, we have on one side the structure of the SDS and on the other side the structure of the administration of Republika Srpska. You will see in common, Radovan Karadzic is both President of the SDS and also the President in the Presidency. The Main Board, you will see Aleksa Buha, member of the Main Board. He was also the Minister of Foreign Affairs in the Assembly. There is a list of names of members of the Assembly; 14 of the members of the Assembly were members of the Main Board. I think from that you will see it is a significant mirroring of power between the SDS leadership and the leadership of the Bosnian Serb administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ralston. What was the role of Dr. Karadzic in the newly formed Bosnian Serb administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was the President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he retain his leadership role in the SDS after becoming the President of the Bosnian Serb administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he became president of the Bosnian Serb administration, he was vested with a number of powers. Do you have some exhibits, Mr. Ralston, that describe those powers? Specifically, let me refer you to Exhibits No. 18 and 20, Exhibit 32 and Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not have 18 and 20 but I am familiar with those documents. I have Exhibit 32. I might add that Dr. Karadzic's position as the leader gave him authority and control over both the civilian and military administration. This, in effect, gave him supreme authority over the police, the Territorial Defence and the Bosnian Serb army. In Exhibit No. 32, which is the law on National Defence, if you go to Article 6 of that Exhibit, it sets out, amongst other things: "The President of the Republic shall ensure unity and indivisibility of the national defence system in the republic; supervise the Territorial Defence both in peace and wartime". It goes on further to say: "He shall issue orders for the utilization of the police in the case of war". If we go later to Article 39, I think it is, Article 39 sets out: "The President of the Republic shall order deployment of Territorial Defence units for the maintenance of law and order in cases of immediate peril of war and other emergency situations". If I now go to Exhibit 33, which is the law on internal affairs, if you go to Article 25, Article 25 sets out, amongst others things: "The President of the Republic shall evaluate the execution of the work programme of the national security service on the basis of a report by the Minister and shall inform the National Assembly thereof". Later in the same document, Article 33, it sets out that, "The Ministry of Internal Affairs shall activate the reserve police in emergency cases as ordered by the President of the Republic".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, what was the effect of these legal documents that you have just testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The effect of these documents is that it gave Dr. Karadzic de jure authority and control over all the official Serb forces in time of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of those powers that you have described, can you provide the court with some examples of his exercise of those powers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He exercised those powers throughout the conflict, an example as late as July 1995, as reported in the media, Bosnian Serb television prime news, set out: "The President of the Republika Srpska and the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, has extraordinarily promoted Major General Milenko Zivanovic, who until recently was the commander of the Drina Corps, into the rank of Lieutenant General. The Republika Srpska Bureau for Press Contacts announced that General Zivanovic has been promoted due to his retirement from active military service". According to the announcement, President Karadzic has appointed the recent Chief of Staff, Major General Radislav Krstic, as the new commander of the Drina Corps who, together with General Zivanovic, was a main architect of the Serbian victories in Srebrenica and Zepa. President Karadzic congratulated the VRS General Staff, the Drina Corps command and the police staff within the armed forces on their brilliant victories in Srebrenica and Zepa, as well as their breaking down of the Muslim offensive on Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic put the police and army under unified command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He stated publicly that the army and the police were put under a unified command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show the court now a film that has been prepared in respect of the answer that Mr. Ralston just provided. If we could please play Exhibit No. 29, clip 2, please? (Exhibit 29, clip 2, was played). Mr. Ralston, as the Commander-in-Chief, had Dr. Karadzic repeatedly backed the actions of his military commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had. I give you a June 1995 example: Dr. Karadzic was interviewed by the BBC in relation to the taking of UN peace keepers as hostages earlier that month. Dr. Karadzic said to the BBC that he was wrong to approve the hostage taking of the UN peace keepers, but he said it was a reasonable reaction to NATO air strikes. "We had to do something very drastic to prevent further strikes and to show the international community that we are cornered and ready to defend ourselves by all means. We function as a state, and I am Commander-in-Chief, supreme Commander, and everything my army do, I do back".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the war, Mr. Ralston, has Dr. Karadzic been dealt with as the leader of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he has. In the course of investigations conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor, investigators and researchers have interviewed various officials who have dealt with Dr. Karadzic since the beginning of the conflict. In addition, there has been extensive research of documents and public statements made by Dr. Karadzic. From the outset he has repeated asserted his position as President of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, or the leader of the Bosnian Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would turn the court's attention to Exhibit No. 34 which is an affidavit signed by Dr. Karadzic. It is an affidavit that was filed in a civil law suit in the United States, Federal District Court. In that particular exhibit you can see THAT Dr. Karadzic asserts his position as President of the Republika Srpska. (To the witness): Mr. Ralston, let me ask you then -- were you going to show that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to show that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will read the relevant portion to the court. "I, Radovan Karadzic, state as follows: I am the President of the Republic of Srpska". It goes on to describe when he was born. In the third, the last sentence of the third paragraph: "I had not visited the United States for any purpose since 1975 until after I became President of Republika Srpska on May 13, 1992".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, since the beginning of the conflict, Dr. Karadzic, as the paramount leader of the Bosnian Serbs, has he been involved in negotiations with the other parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he has. It must be recognised that many of these negotiations were conducted by means of shuttle diplomacy, but I can provide some examples of this. On 24th January 1992, he attended a debate on a referendum of independence. The main people in the debate were Mr. Izetbegovic for the SDA, Dr. Karadzic for the SDS and Mr. Kljuic for the HDZ. On 12th April 1992, he was involved in negotiations on a cease fire in Sarajevo. He agreed to the cease fire. On 2nd June 1992, Karadzic was involved in negotiations over the opening of Sarajevo airport. During 1992 and 1993, Dr. Karadzic participated in negotiations conducted under the auspices of the national conference for former Yugoslavia. On 18th November 1993, he signed a joint declaration on humanitarian assistance along with Mr. H. Silajdzic and Mr. M. Boban. On 6th March 1994, he had a meeting with UNPROFOR officials concerning an overall cease fire. From 2nd to 6th June 1994, he was involved in Geneva talks on the cessation of hostilities. An agreement was reached in those talks. In December 1994, he was involved in negotiations on cease fire and cessation of hostilities with former US President, Jimmy Carter. An agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I would like to refer you to Exhibits 35, 36, 37, 38 and 39. I will give you a moment just to get those exhibits. Let me ask you if you can identify each of those exhibits and explain to the court the significance of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 35 is a document signed by Mr. D. Kalinic, "Representative of Dr. Karadzic, President of the Serbian Democratic Party". The group of people mentioned in the document, a representative of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a representative -- a further representative of the SDS, a representative of the SDA and a representative of the HDZ met in Geneva on 22nd May 1992 on application or dealing with the "application and implementation of international humanitarian law within the context of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina". They reached an agreement in relation to those topics. Exhibit 36 is an agreement reached on 5th June 1992 on the reopening of Sarajevo airport for humanitarian purposes. This exhibit was signed by Dr. Karadzic. Exhibit 37 is an instruction issued to Serbian forces around the town of Gorazde to begin an immediate unilateral cease fire, again signed by Dr. Karadzic on 16th July 1992. Exhibit 38 is a joint declaration for humanitarian assistance signed by Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Silajdzic, Mr. Boban. Finally, Exhibit 39 is a cessation of hostilities agreement which followed the negotiations with US President Carter -- US former President Carter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described, Mr. Ralston, a broad range of agreements that were signed by Dr. Karadzic as the leader of the Republika Srpska; were these agreements implemented, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For example, the agreement on the reopening of Sarajevo airport and the cessation of hostility agreement following the Carter negotiations and also the agreement for one month's suspension of military offensives following the Geneva conference in June 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, thank you for your testimony in regards to Dr. Karadzic. I would now like to turn for a few minutes to the other person named in the two indictments, General Mladic. Could you please tell the court who he is and give a description of his background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic received his training at the military academy in the former Yugoslavia and was a career JNA officer before he became the commander of the Bosnian Serb army. His first assignment as an officer in November 1965 was as a platoon commander in Skopje, Macedonia. Between 1989 and 1991, Mladic served as the head of the Education Department of the Third Military District. From January through June 1991, he was the Deputy Commander of the Pristina Corps in Kosovo. In June 1991, the JNA General Staff sent Mladic to Knin as commander of the Knin Corps. At the time the JNA was fighting various Croatian forces. Approximately two months after Mladic arrived in Knin, the JNA promoted him to Brigadier General because of his combat exploits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he leave the JNA and become the commander of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This occurred in the second half of April 1992. General Mladic and others were formed of this decision by the SFRY Presidency. They were told that they were reassigned from their present posts to new posts at the command of the Second Military District, the Second Military District centred in Sarajevo. The new posts were as follows: Major General Ratko Mladic was appointed Chief of Staff of the Second Military District; Major General Milan Gvero, assistant commander for morale and information; Colonel Gruber, assistant commander for organisational and mobilization and personnel issues, and the late General Djorde Dukic, assistant commander for logistics. Shortly after these posts were transferred to the Bosnian Serb army. This information was confirmed by General Djorde Dukic in interviews with representatives of the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He stated to the authorities: "I know that the SFRY Government made a decision in May or June 1992 for all federal reserves on the territory of Republika Srpska to be transferred to the jurisdiction of the Government of Republika Srpska which was then called Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. "As regards the consolidation of units and the creation of the Army of the Republika Srpska, I can state that almost all units of the JNA had withdrawn from the territory of Republika Srpska by 19th May 1992, and by the end of June even the smallest groups had withdrawn. These did not include individuals of Serbian nationality born on the territory Bosnia and Herzegovina".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a direct quote from General Dukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. At the time Mladic became the Commander of the District, the commanding JNA Generals, Stankovic and Kukanjac, were returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did General Mladic do when he received notice that the JNA was officially going to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladic in interview with a Knin magazine in Belgrade indicated that he had received advance warning that the JNA was going to withdraw officially from Bosnia-Herzegovina. He immediately started to establish his own command structure. In the Knin magazine Mladic described his efforts as follows: "As soon as I took over duty in the Second Military District, I set my aim at gathering people and establishing the Command and the Main Staff, some from people of the Second Military District and some from the people who had come with me from Knin and other areas, who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. "As soon as the decision was made on 19th May 1992 for the JNA to retreat from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we met at the highest military and political levels and decided to establish the Serb Army and the Main Staff. The Army was founded at the Bosnian Serb Assembly session in Banja Luka on 11th and 12th May. I went to Banja Luka and met with President Dr. Radovan Karadzic and his representatives. They told me that a decision was made for me to take over the duty of Commander".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, can you briefly describe to the court how the BSA was structured and identify the relevant persons in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to Exhibit 40. If you look at the structure, the highest position in the army is General Ratko Mladic; immediately down to him is his Deputy, Major Gvero. Underneath General Mladic is his main staff; Major General Milanovic is the Chief of Staff; Major General Martic, the assistant commander for air defence; Lieutenant General Dukic, assistant commander for logistics; Major General Skrbic, assistant commander for mobilization and personnel and Major General Zdravko Tolimir who is assistant commander for intelligence. Immediately also directly under General Mladic were the Corps commands First Krajina Corps led by General Talic; Second Krajina Corps led initially by General Boric and later General Tomanic; the Third Krajina Corps, Colonel Lisica; the East Bosnia Corps, General Simic; the Drina Corps, initially, General Zivanovic and then General Krstic; the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was initially commanded by General Sipcic, later General Galic and then General Milosevic and the Herzegovina Corps commanded by General Grubac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, let me ask you in respect of these Corps that you have described, did they operate in specific geographic regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I refer you to the second part of this Exhibit. You will see here that the three Krajina Corps, the first, second and third, operated in these districts; the East Bosnian Corps in this district, the Drina Corps in this area here; the Herzegovina Corps here and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you explain the relationship between Dr. Karadzic, the President of the Bosnian Serb administration, and General Mladic who was the Commander of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was his supreme commander. From interviews with former UNPROFOR officials who, at various stages of the conflict were based in Sarajevo, it is clear that from the outset Dr. Karadzic was the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs and had control over the military. It is also clear that from as early as 14th May 1992, General Ratko Mladic was in effective control of the military. Although Mladic acted and thought independently and demonstrated absolute control over his troops, he would defer to Karadzic as the overall leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to being the military commander, did he also represent the Bosnian Serb administration in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He participated in negotiations and made agreements principally in relation to military matters on issues such as demilitarisation, cease fires and cessation of combat activities and cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you provide the court with some information about the types of agreements he negotiated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On 2nd June 1992, with Dr. Karadzic, he was involved in negotiations on the agreement to open Sarajevo airport. Bosnian Serb forces under his control held the area around the airport. This agreement was subsequently signed and implemented. On 5th June, Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic were involved in negotiations with the Bosnian Serb Presidency over the airport being placed under UN control. On 30th July 1993, Mladic was involved in negotiations with General Briquemont, Generals Delic and Petkovic and defined an agreement -- signed an agreement to define safe areas. On 11th August 1993, Mladic signed an agreement with General -- sorry, on 14th August, Mladic reached an agreement with General Briquemont concerning Mount Igman and the withdrawal of Bosnian Serb forces. On 8th February 1994, General Milovanovic, a representative of General Mladic, met with General Sir Michael Rose in Lukavica to discuss cease fire, withdrawal of heavy weapons and the subsequent demilitarisation of Sarajevo. Milovanovic said that he had the full authority from Karadzic and Mladic to agree to the principles of the cease fire. The following day, General Sir Michael Rose met with Milovanovic who agreed to a cease fire. There was no document signed but the cease fire held. On 15th April 1994, negotiations between Rose and General Mladic were held regarding Gorazde. On 22nd April, General Milovanovic signed an agreement on Gorazde. The agreement was a general cease fire. There were also numerous meetings where his representatives met with others and reached agreement on various issues, including humanitarian convoys and anti-sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have provided in your binders Exhibits 41, 42, 43, 44 and 39. I will not ask Mr. Ralston any questions about these agreements, but these are examples of agreements that were negotiated and signed by General Mladic. Lastly, Mr. Ralston, let me ask you if the agreements which were negotiated and signed by General Mladic were, in fact, implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The best example are the Sarajevo airport agreements and the agreements following the Carter negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your description and your testimony about General Mladic. I would like to turn to another subject now, Mr. Ralston. I would like to turn your attention to the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina starting in 1992. Was the occupation and control of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia by the Bosnian Serbs well planned and executed, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The occupation and control of territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the self-styled "Republika Srpska" was well-planned and co-ordinated. The planning by the Bosnian Serb political leaders of the SDS and others was executed in coordination with the military and paramilitary forces, the police and local Bosnian Serbs. The goal was to secure complete control over the territory which they considered to be Serbian in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, has the investigation revealed any patterns of pre-takeover and post-takeover conduct by the Bosnian Serb forces under the direction and control of Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In those portions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, a consistent pattern of pre- takeover and post-takeover conduct emerged. This pattern reflect a high degree of central control and planning by those responsible for the take-over. In areas where the Bosnian Serbs represented a large majority of the population, control was achieved quickly and with limited use of force. In other areas, where Bosnian Serbs did not have such a majority, it was achieved by the use of substantial force, including heavy shelling of villages and towns follow by infantry attack. In either case, what followed for the non-Serb population was brutal and swift repression and persecution on discriminatory grounds. Thousands of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were rounded up, detained in internment facilities run by the Bosnian Serb military, the police or both. The conditions in these facilities were brutal -- detainees were murdered, tortured, physically abused, raped and sexually assaulted. Daily food rations and hygienic conditions were grossly inadequate. For those non-Serbs who did not end up in the detention facilities, life in their communities included systematic dismissal from employment, restraint on freedom of movement, appropriation of property, destruction of their homes and businesses, physical abuse, including murder, rape, and torture, arbitrary arrest, deportation and other conditions that made remaining in their homes precarious at best.
