Muslim and catholic places of worship have been damaged or destroyed in significant numbers throughout the occupied territories as well. These patterns I have described have been substantiated by in-depth investigations conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor in regard to the Bosnian Serb takeovers that occurred in the municipalities of Sarajevo, Foca, Bosanski Samac, Vlasenica, Brcko and Prijedor. The patterns are further supported by information provided to the OTP in relation to events that occurred in Kotor Varos, Bijeljina, Zvornik and other areas. Throughout the conflict, tactics used by the Bosnian Serb military have included both indiscriminate and direct targeting of civilians. The siege of Sarajevo typifies these tactics. Since the beginning of the siege, civilians in that city were subjected to indiscriminate fire by weapons such as mortars, rockets and artillery as well as a systematic sniper campaign that has resulted in a high number of casualities".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, before the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the territory that is now occupied by the Bosnian Serbs, were there municipalities where the Bosnian Serbs represented a minority of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as is well known, the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the conflict consisted largely of five national groups, Serbians, Croatians, Muslims, Yugoslavs and others. Whilst over half of the municipalities in the area claimed by the Bosnian Serbs had a Serbian majority, many did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit No. 45 in your binders is a summary of the 1991 census, and it will substantiate what Mr. Ralston has just testified about. Mr. Ralston, I would like you to please turn to Exhibit No. 46 and ask you to identify and explain to the court what it represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map shows you, firstly, confrontation line as at July 1995. Behind that confrontation line is largely the area which was controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. The areas in pink are the areas which had -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am very sorry. Maybe we could turn down the lights just a little bit because it is hard really to see what is on the map, so if that were possible? If we could just dim the light a little bit? We all have the same problem indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will repeat what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Wait just a minute until the lights are dimmed, Mr. Ralston. All right. Mr. Ralston, please proceed with your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, the green line roughly marks the confrontation line as of July 1995. The areas in behind that line are the areas which are controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. Now, the areas shaded in pink are the areas that as in the 1991 census showed a non-Serb majority population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you now turn to Exhibit No. 47, identify it and explain its significance to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 47 is a document which is headed "Serbian Democratic Party Bosnia-Herzegovina, Main Committee, strictly confidential". It is instructions for the organisation and activities of the organs of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a state of emergency. The significance of this document is on 19th December 1991 a special Crisis Staff of the SDS issued these "strictly confidential" instructions. Noting that certain forces were working to take Bosnia-Herzegovina out of Yugoslavia by force, the Crisis Staff saw the necessity for working out "unified tasks, measures and other activities" for the purposes of carrying out the decision of the Bosnian Serb plebiscite as well as in other circumstances which might arise in the development of the political and security situation. The instructions provided for the conduct of specified in all municipalities in which Serbs lived. This was to occur in two variants depending on whether Serbs formed majority (Variant A) or not (Variant B). In both variants, the municipal committee of the SDS was to admittedly form a Crisis Staff composed of all members of the secretariat of the communal committee of the SDS, leading communal officials or SDS candidates for those positions (chairman of the Assembly or of the Executive Committee, chief of the public security or militia station, Commander of the Territorial Defence staff, secretary of the secretariat of National Defence), deputies to the Assembly of the Serbian people and local members of the Main Committee of the SDS. The commander of the Crisis Staff was to be the chairman of the communal assembly/executive committee (Variant A) or the chairman of the communal committee of the SDS (Variant B). The Crisis Staffs were responsible for monitoring the political situation in the municipality and making preparations to take over all governmental functions, including the gathering of supplies in secret depots and mobilisation of men into the police, Territorial Defence and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The significance of this document, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document contains a number of instructions on the organisation and activities of Bosnian Serbs and the municipal and Local Commune levels. The instructions were given by the Crisis Staff of the SDS. The instructions would basically prepare the Bosnian Serbs for war on the municipal and commune levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, you mentioned earlier that the Office of the Prosecutor has conducted in-depth investigations in certain municipalities. Can you identify those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo, Foca, Bosanski Samac, Vlasenica, Brcko and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you inform the court what the strategic significance of those municipalities is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps we need the lights dimmed once again, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly, the municipalities of Foca, Bosanski Samac, Vlasenica, Brcko and Prijedor all had substantial non-Serb majority population. If you look at the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, firstly, you will notice that the terrain is extremely rugged. Because of the ruggedness of this terrain, the transport thoroughfares were particularly significant. If you look at Foca, you will see that it stands at the junction of the major highway which connects between Montenegro and Belgrade, Herzegovina and the coast. If you go to Brcko, sorry, to Vlasenica, you will see that Vlasenica is the main road and rail link between Serbia and Sarajevo. The rail link comes to the border and then there is the road link through Vlasenica to Sarajevo. Brcko stands in probably the most critical area for the Bosnian Serbs. This area, as I said, was a non-Serb majority area, but it was through this road network here that Serbs in Eastern Bosnia and Serbia could connect with Serbs in Western Bosnia and the parts of Croatian Krajina which at that stage were controlled by the Serbs. So it is a complete -- it is a very significant military objective. If you come across just a little bit further to Bosanski Samac which is about here, it also stood on the edge of the Posavina corridor, which is the area through Brcko, and the same road and rail links. If you come across to Prijedor, you will notice that the rail link between the east Serbia and the western areas go straight through Prijedor, as does the major highway. So, for each of these municipalities, in addition to being predominantly non-Serbs surrounded by Serb controlled areas, they were also particularly important because of the transport thoroughfares that went through them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you turn to Exhibit No. 49 as well and put that on the screen? Mr. Ralston, after the war started, can you tell me what happened in the municipality that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, these were particularly significant municipalities, and you can see that each of these municipalities was taken over by the Serbs very early in the conflict, Foca on 6th April, Bosanski Samac on 17th April, Brcko -- sorry, then Vlasenica on 21st April and then, finally, Prijedor on 25th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned that the Office of the Prosecutor has conducted in-depth investigations in many of those municipalities. Could you please describe to the court what happened in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before the conflict, Sarajevo had developed as a flourishing multi-ethnic city. On 5th April, following demonstrations and peace marches, fighting broke out with gun fire and explosions heard throughout the city. On 6th April, sniper fire was reported originating from the Holiday Inn near the centre of the city. The Holiday Inn at that time was the headquarters of the SDS party and was occupied -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you, but perhaps before discussing Sarajevo, we could proceed to a recess, unless there is a very short answer, but I have the feeling that we are being to be talking about this for sometime so maybe we could have a recess first. As it is 4 o'clock, it would be a good time. I am very sorry, Mr. Ralston, to interrupt you. So the session is adjourned until 4.15. (4.00 p.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (4.20 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First, I would like to turn to the Prosecutor and I would like to inform him that the Chamber accepts the documents you tendered so far as exhibits. We will make sure that we do the same for the forthcoming exhibits. Still dealing with some concrete or material problems, I was told by the interpreters that they find it difficult hearing the Prosecutor because he stands up far away from the microphone. These may be sound like a small problem, and yet they make the interpreters' work more difficult. So when the presiding Judge makes the interpreters' job difficult, he apologises, he does whatever he can. Now it turns out that the Judges have nothing to do with that. Apparently, these problems have been mentioned since the opening of the Tadic case. It is probably a technical thing that can probably easily be fixed, but it appears that if you have to bend over it will be very difficult for you, Prosecutor. But, anyway, we simply wanted to point out that we should make sure to have the appropriate working conditions for everybody. As far as the Judges are concerned, all conditions are very good, but that should apply to everybody. So I will ask the representatives of the Registry to make sure that if it does not involve too much work, could that be fixed as soon as possible? I am speaking here on behalf of Mrs. MacDonald who is the Presiding Judge for the Tadic case and on our behalf. So, Prosecutor, I think we can resume now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. (To the witness): When we had left off, Mr. Ralston, I had asked you whether or not the Office of the Prosecutor had conducted in-depth investigations in certain municipalities and you answered that they had and you had identified those municipalities. My next question was to ask you what had happened in those municipalities. You started out with a description and a brief summary of what occurred in Sarajevo. Could you please continue your answer as to what occurred in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will, I will repeat the last couple of sentences that I said. Before the conflict, Sarajevo had developed as a flourishing multi-ethnic city. On 6th April 1992, sniper fire was reported originating from the Holiday Inn near the centre of the city. The Holiday Inn at that time was the headquarters of the SDS party, and was occupied by party officials and body guards, as well as a number of international journalists and UNPROFOR members. A number of people were killed and injured by this initial fire. The following day, 7th April 1992, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by the European Community and the United States. From May 1992 until the end of the conflict, Sarajevo was subjected to a siege by the Bosnian Serb forces. During the siege, the civilian population suffered greatly from the continued and systematic sniper attacks by Bosnian Serb forces and from the indiscriminate and intensive use of mortar and artillery fire. As a result, thousands of civilians, regardless of age or gender, have been killed or injured. Shelling attacks have directly targeted civilians engaged in clearly non-combat activities. Hospitals, cemeteries and cultural buildings have regularly been targeted, as have the personnel and property of humanitarian aid and peacekeeping bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you please summarise what our investigations have shown in relation to the municipality of Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Foca municipality, as I indicated previously, was an area which had a majority non-Serb population. According to the 1991 census, of the population of 40,513, 51.6 per cent were Muslim, 45.3 per cent Serb and 3.1 per cent classified as "others". The political and military takeover of Foca started in early April. The first military actions in the town were reported on 6th April 1992 when Serbian military units took over Foca section by section. The occupation of the town of Foca was complete by 16th or 17th April. The surrounding villages were under siege until some time in July 1992 before they were also overtaken. During an after the takeover, a number of the non-Serb population were detained, interrogated, beaten and held in inhumane conditions in detention facilities run by the Serbian authorities. Women were separated from the men and were held in different detention centres where rapes were frequently committed by guards and other Serbs. Later, many of the non-Serbs were taken from these facilities and exchanged in so-called "prisoner exchanges" or deported, mainly to Montenegro. Many non-Serbian residents were murdered. During the months after the takeover, the living conditions, including the fear of being killed, became so unbearable that many non-Serbs, who had managed to avoid detention, decided to leave the area. Those people who left were forced to sign papers saying they were leaving Foca of their own volition and that they were voluntarily handing over all their possessions to the Serb authorities. By admission of the Serbian authorities, as of August 1993, there were only nine Muslims left in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, would you please describe what the Office of the Prosecutor's investigations have shown in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Bosanski Samac, as you will recall, was at the edge of the Posavina corridor. Before the war, the population of Bosanski Samac was made up almost evenly divided between Croats and Serbs, with Muslims making up a small minority. According to the 1991 census, the municipality had a total population of 32,835 people, of whom 45 per cent were Croats, 41 per cent Serbs, 7 per cent Muslims and 7 per cent "others". Before the war, most of the Croatian residents lived in several predominantly Croatian outlying villages. Muslims constituted the majority in the town of Bosanski Samac, and there were some villages with ethnically mixed populations. Early on the morning of 17th April 1992, Serbian military forces seized control of Bosanski Samac. Shortly after the attack members of these units went from house to house with lists of non-Serbian residents and ordered all non-Serbs to turn in their weapons. Irregular forces swept through the town looting homes. Some homes, community buildings and villages were destroyed. Many non-Serbs were immediately arrested and detained in detention facilities set up in several different locations around the town of Bosanski Samac, including one in the local police station. In those detention facilities, beatings and mistreatment were a daily occurrence. Some of the detainees were killed, others were subjected to humiliating sexual assaults. Overnight, Bosnian Serbs took control of all businesses and government offices, and assumed all positions of authority. As it occurred hundreds of kilometres away in Foca, the Serbian authorities proceeded to reduce the civilian non-Serbian population by imposing brutal conditions. Non-Serbs were arrested, detained, beaten, tortured, murdered and humiliated. Those not arrested or detained lived in fear, under such oppressive conditions, that many chose to leave the area to escape the intolerable situation. Many civilians were used in "prisoner exchanges". By March 1995 it was estimated that about 10 Croats and 250 Muslims remained in the municipality. As of July 1995, 98 per cent of the non-Serb population had either left or been deported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you summarise for the court what the Prosecutor's investigations have shown in relation to the municipality of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to Vlasenica, again non-Serbs were the majority population. The municipality had approximately 33,817 citizens, of whom approximately 55 per cent were Muslim, 43 per cent Serb and 2 per cent described as "other". The town of Vlasenica is located in the municipality of the same name. In 1991, the town of Vlasenica had approximately 7,500 citizens, of whom approximately 4,800 or 64 per cent were Muslim. In the months leading up to the takeover of the municipality of Vlasenica, there was considerable tension between Bosnian Serb and non-Serbian officials. The tension related primarily to SDS demands for various forms of political control. Ultimately, the SDS demanded that Vlasenica be divided into Serbian and non-Serbian areas. Significantly, just before the takeover, Serbs had begun to set up a separate administration and police force. Serbian paramilitary groups moved into the area and the Muslim population was ordered to hand over their weapons. On 21st April 1992, the Bosnian Serb takeover of Vlasenica was effected by members of the Novi Sad Corps of the JNA assisted by paramilitary units. Following the takeover of the town of Vlasenica, the remaining Muslim villages in the municipality were also captured and civilians were arrested, mistreated, detained in camps or deported. Many of the civilians' homes were destroyed. After the takeover, detention warrants and criminal charges were drawn up against the Muslim leaders and SDS members of the area -- SDA members of the area, I am sorry , but by that time 95 per cent of the Muslim officials had fled. On the day of the takeover of the town of Vlasenica, Serbs in a police car forced a Muslim religious leader to give an ultimatum to the non-Serb population in which they were instructed to hand over all weapons. During and after the takeover, non-Serbian villages were attacked and the Muslim residents rounded up and detained. In addition, the Serbian forces destroyed and looted much of the Muslim property. Once the civilians were detained, the men and women were separated. The women were deported and the men were detained for extended periods of time in inhumane conditions. The men were interrogated and beaten for no apparent reason. After being released from detention, some of the men were used for "prisoners exchanges". Many of the civilians detained were subsequently sent to the Batkovic camp in north east Bosnia where they were detained for lengthy periods. Most of Muslim women, driven by fear, were compelled to sign documents stating they were leaving the area of their own free will. Prior to leaving, however, the people had to obtain permission to leave from the Serbian run Crisis Staff and had to sign over all their property to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, did similar events occur in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. In Brcko, the population was approximately 87,000 with 43,000 inhabitants residing in the town of Brcko itself. The population of the municipality was 45 per cent Muslim; 20.7 per cent Serb; 25.9 per cent Croat; 5.5 per cent Yugoslav and 3 per cent "other". So it can be seen that the Serbian population was the significant minority in this area. However, as I have previously stated, control of this area was vital to the Bosnian Serb programme. The war in Brcko began in the early morning of 30th April 1992, when powerful explosions destroyed the two bridges across the Sava River. Immediately thereafter, the SDS Crisis Staff assumed power in the municipality. On 1st May 1992, the post office, radio and television stations and the police station were taken over by soldiers wearing the uniform of the JNA. Residents who tried to leave the town were turned back at checkpoints manned by Serbian soldiers and paramilitary soldiers known as Arkanovci or Seseljevci, which were controlled by Zeljko Raznjatovic "Arkan" and Vojislav Seselj respectively. On 2nd May 1992, shooting began in the predominantly Muslim neighbourhoods of Dizdarusa, Kolobara and Klanac as Muslim fighters organised a resistance to the Serbian soldiers in the town. An artillery bombardment began in the Muslim neighbourhoods and residents sought shelter in the basements of their homes. Houses were damaged severely as a result of the shelling. On 3rd May 1992, Serbian soldiers began moving through the city, forcing residents to leave their homes and to "evacuate to safe areas". Muslim and Croat residents were separated from Serbs and taken to collection centres. Women, children and the elderly were separated from the men and bused out of Brcko to Brezevo Polje, a village a few kilometres east of the town of Brcko. While at the collection centres, Muslims and Croats were subjected to verbal harassment, physical beatings and some were killed. A large percentage of the non-Serbian male population was detained at the Luka camp in the town of Brcko where beatings, torture and murder were common place. The camp authorities executed detainees on a systematic basis during the first weeks of Luka's operation. In July, all male detainees were bused to the nearby Batkovic detention camp. Other non-Serbian males, who had previously been detained and released, were later re-arrested and also taken to Batkovic. As a result of the climate of fear and terror created by the Serbian actions, the overwhelming majority of non-Serbian residents who were not killed or detained left the area by any means possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you describe what the Prosecutor's investigations have shown in relation to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecutor's office has conducted extensive investigations in relation to events in the Prijedor area. Prijedor, before May 1991, was almost evenly divided between Muslims and Serbs. According to the 1991 census, the municipality had a total population of 112,470 people, of whom 44 per cent were Muslim, 42.5 per cent Serb, 5.6 per cent Croats, 5.7 per cent Yugoslav and 2.2 per cent described as "others". I am told the "others" are often made up of Ukrainians, Russians and Italians. On 30th April 1992, Bosnian Serb forces seized power in the town of Prijedor. There was no meaningful resistance, as non-Serb police surrendered their arms to their Serbian colleagues. The following morning, Serbian flags flew from all official buildings and Radio Prijedor broadcast that Serbs had taken over the municipality, which was henceforth to be called "Serbian Municipality Prijedor". Over the next three weeks, Radio Prijedor repeatedly broadcast demands that non-Serbs surrender all remaining arms, even licensed hunting weapons. Muslim officials met with Bosnian Serb authorities to negotiate a peaceful co-existence. During this time, travel for non-Serbs was increasingly curtailed and communication lines from predominantly Muslim villages to the outside world were cut. Before and after the Bosnian Serbs seized power, they supplied arms and weapons to the Serbian villages in the municipality. Heavy weapons were also introduced into the area. Military attacks in the Prijedor municipality began on 23rd May 1992, after an incident at a checkpoint near the village of Hambarine. Military attacks on Hambarine and Ljubija were followed by attacks on Kozarac and Prijedor town. Beginning on 20th July 1992, villages on the left bank of the Sana River were attacked by Serbian forces. As in most of the other attacks, the left bank villages were subjected to heavy shelling, followed by a mass round up and killings of non-Serbian civilians. Many homes and villages were destroyed during and after the attacks, making it impossible for people to return to the villages. Those who were arrested and detained endured long term detention in facilities marked by the cruel and inhumane treatment of inmates. Many thousands of non-Serbian civilians suffered in the infamous detention camps of Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje. From these centres the detainees were later either transferred to the Manjaca camp and from there to either Batkovic camp or to other areas outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those who were not detained lived under such oppressive conditions and in such a state of fear that most eventually left Prijedor. By June 1993, 88 per cent of the Muslim population of approximately 49,000 had been killed or forced to leave the area. Today the majority of the previous non-Serbian population in the Prijedor municipality has been expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, you have testified that as a result of the events that took place in those respective municipalities, the ethnic composition of each of those municipalities changed. Would you please refer to Exhibit No. 50? I would ask you, once it is put on the elmo, to please identify and explain its relevance to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have the lights down at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the municipalities of Prijedor, Foca, Vlasenica, Brcko and Bosanski Samac, of which I have just spoken, the population changed from being a Serbian minority to being almost totally Serbian. A research indicates that this occurred in other areas taken over as well, for example, Kotor Varos, Sanski Most, Doboj, Visegrad and several of the areas along here. I will also indicate that Bosnian Serbs also took control of these areas in here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, you have described a number of the methods that were used by the forces that took over these particular municipalities. Could you please explain what common features you found, what patterns you found, in terms of those methods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The common features include initially ultimatums, to hand over weapons, to swear allegiance to the Bosnian Serb administration and the surrender of certain individuals. There were military attacks followed by wholesale destruction of villages. It was indiscriminate murder, separation of men from the women, children and the elderly, incarceration in various forms of detention facilities. These detention facilities were either run by the police, military authorities or both. At these facilities interrogations, beatings, murder, sexual assault were commonplace, as was torture. Many of the those incarcerated were later subjected to deportation, as were civilians who were not detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those methods, Mr. Ralston, before we turn to them specifically, occurred in municipalities that were located all throughout the territory occupied by the Bosnian Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned one of the patterns that has emerged in the course of the Prosecutor's investigations is that ultimatums were a common feature in takeovers; could you please explain to the court what you mean by that and give the court some examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ultimatums were frequently issued by the SDS, the members of the Bosnian Serb army, or the police, to representatives of the Muslim villages to surrender their arms. To illustrate this, I will provide you with an example from Prijedor: on 22nd May 1992, a car with five men, four Serbs and a Croat, were stopped at a checkpoint in the village of Hambarine near Prijedor. When the Serbs were asked to surrender their weapons, one of the Serbs opened fire with his machine gun. The commander at the checkpoint was wounded and later died of his wounds. The other non-Serbs at the checkpoint returned fire and killed two of the Serbs. The Serbs then asked the non-Serbs to surrender themselves and the checkpoint. After the shooting incident, the SDS Crisis Staff in Prijedor delivered an ultimatum over Radio Prijedor in which they demanded that the men who they held responsible for the shooting at the checkpoint be handed over to them, and that all weapons in Hambarine be surrendered to the Serbs. If the ultimatum was not met by noon the following day, the Serbs said they would attack Hambarine. When the ultimatum was not met, the Serbs commenced an artillery bombardment of Hambarine. When the artillery fire ceased, the village was attacked by tanks and infantry and houses were set on fire. When the attack on Hambarine started, large numbers of villagers fled to other nearby Muslim or Croatian villages. Others took to the woods and remained there until they thought the immediate danger was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the ultimatum was issued by the Prijedor Crisis Staff, what happened to the village of Hambarine and other nearby villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as in the above example, ultimatums were delivered both by the SDS run Crisis Staff, civil officials and members of the military forces. In relation to Hambarine, later that day negotiations between Major Radmilo Zeljaja and Becir Medunjanin, a representative of the Muslim community of Kozarac, were monitored on the police radio in Kozarac. Zeljaja issued an ultimatum that the people of Kozarac either sign a pledge of loyalty to the Bosnian Serb Republic and hand over all weapons or Kozarac would be attacked. Zeljaja informed Medunjanin that he had until noon for the ultimatum to be reached. About noon on 24th May 1992, Becir Medunjanin asked for more time, but Zeljaja told him that time had run out. Shortly thereafter, Kozarac was attacked by local Serbs from Lamovita and Omarska and troops from the Banja Luka Corps under the command of Colonel Vladimir Arsic and Major Zeljaja, the commander in the field. Kozarac town and the villages of Kamicani, Jakupovici and Kozarusa were subjected to heavy bombardment by artillery, and from tanks and smaller weapons. On 27th May 1992, Bosnian-Serb army tanks and infantry moved into Kozarac and, as the local population had not organised any real resistance to the attack, the Serbs moved in virtually unimpeded. Many of the inhabitants of the area fled to the nearby forests of the Kozara Mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those individuals, Mr. Ralston, who fled into the woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the shelling stopped, the surrender of thousands of the inhabitants of the Kozarac area was negotiated by a number of the former Muslim police and Major Zeljaja. Many people, men women and children, took advantage of this surrender, formed columns and moved towards Prijedor town under the guard of the Serbian forces. As the column was moving along the road many of the men were taken from the column and killed on the spot. The Muslim commander of the police in Kozarac and a number of his officers were killed after they were surrendered. At a checkpoint along the road the column was met by Bosnian Serb forces and the men were separated from the women and children. The majority of the men were then placed on buses and taken to the Omarska and Keraterm camps. The majority of the women and children were taken to Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, you mentioned that one of the patterns that the investigations have revealed is a pattern of murder of civilians by the police and military personnel. Can you please expand on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the municipalities mentioned, summary execution of civilians both inside and outside of the detention facilities was commonplace. Perhaps the best or most graphic examples of this occurred in Brcko where a photographer happened to be on the scene and captured photographs of the murder of two apparently civilian people. These photographs were later published in international media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we have the lights dimmed. Your Honour, we are going to refer now to Exhibits 51A, B and C. If they could be shown now. Could you explain, Mr. Ralston, please what is shown in this Exhibit as soon as we get a focus on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see here two civilians being escorted by an armed man in what appears to be a police uniform and another armed man in what appears to be a military uniform. If we move to the next photograph ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, those photographs were taken in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those photographs were taken in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you move to the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will see in this photograph that the gentleman in the apparently police uniform has raised his weapon. What has occurred here is he has fired into the back of the civilian in front of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please show the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photo graphically depicts what happened to the civilian. I might also add that the other gentleman who is shown, the other civilian shown in the first photograph was murdered at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ralston. If we could have the lights back up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is the next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case we will not have them up. Let me now turn to the next pattern that has been revealed, and that is the destruction of Muslim villages. Is there another photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. Let me go back then to one more photograph in that series.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the same day that that last series of photographs were taken, this photograph of a mass grave near Brcko was taken. You can see that bodies in the grave are all wearing civilian clothes. It is Exhibit No. 52.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now we can have the lights up. Mr. Ralston, let me turn your attention to another feature in the patterns that the Prosecutor's investigations have revealed, and that is the destruction of Muslim villages. Can you please explain to the court what you mean by that and we will turn to some exhibits in just a minute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In general as the Muslim population had been removed from villages, Bosnian Serb forces would come through and destroy their houses to prevent their return. In Vlasenica the attack started, as I said, on 22nd April. Following the official departure of the JNA troops and their replacement by Bosnian Serb troops, Bosnian Serb army troops, Muslim villages continue to be destroyed. The attacks on these villages met with little or no resistance. In many cases people had turned in their weapons. In the Prijedor municipality the following villages suffered from bombardment or total or partial destruction by Serbian military, paramilitary and police units: Hambarine and Ljubija on 22nd May, Kozarac, Alici, Brdjani, Donji Forici, Gornja Forici, Hrnici, Jakupovic, Kamicani, Kevljani, Kenjari, Kozarusa and others, and Prijedor, Tukovi and Stari Grad on 30th May. In a further wave of attacks on 20th July the following villages suffered widespread destruction: Biscani, Karakovo, Rizvanovici, Sredice, Zidovi, Brisevo, Donji Ljubija, Gornji Ljubija, Raljas and Lisina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, let me ask you to refer to Exhibits 53, 54 and 55, and please expand on your testimony using those exhibits, if you would. Before you start, Mr. Ralston, we need to get it on the video screen. Perhaps the lights could be dimmed on this as well. No, they had better stay as bright as they can. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will refer you firstly to the colour coding on the map. The blue indicates populated areas, the yellow destruction from shelling, and the red destruction from fire or explosives. You will see here heavy concentration of red. This red correlates with the Muslims villages of Prijedor which I have just spoken about. You will see in this area here there is also a heavy concentration of red showing large numbers of homes have been destroyed. Our evidence shows that the majority of these houses which have been destroyed from either fires or explosives are on areas which were previously predominantly Muslim. If we move to the next exhibit, if I can show that more graphically in relation to this area here and later this area here. Now this map is a portion of eastern and central Bosnia. The areas in green are the areas which are shown in the 1991 census has been a predominantly Muslim population. You will see in those areas you have indicated by red again where the houses have been destroyed from either fires or explosives. You will see the concentration of destruction of houses by fire and explosives is extremely high in the predominantly Muslim areas. If we move to the next exhibit it will show us something similar which occurred in the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For this we need the lights dimmed. If we could have them dimmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. This map here is the area in north western Bosnia and it encompasses the Prijedor area which I have previously given evidence about, part of Banja Luka and Sanski Most. What these concentrations here show are what are called ethnically cleansed towns. The blue occurred from mid-April to mid-May. You will see here, here and Prijedor town. In May you see the concentration of villages outside of Prijedor I spoke to. From late May to early June you will see that these villages in this area here suffered from ethnic cleansing, and from late July you will see the concentration in these areas here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, in many of these villages there were Serbian people who lived, Bosnian Serbian people who lived next to Bosnian Muslim people. Did it frequently occur that portions of the Muslim community were essentially obliterated and portions of the community that were Bosnian-Serb remained intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that regard, Mr. Ralston, I would like to show you, please, Exhibit 56A and B. I would ask you once it gets put on the elmo to explain what this is an example of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. This is an aerial photograph. What it shows you, and this is in the city of the Foca which I have previously given testimony about, this area here is described as the Serb section of Foca. A short distance away you have a Muslim section. It is not quite so clear from this photograph, but I will show you in a moment. There is no destruction in this area whilst all the buildings in this area have been destroyed. I have two further photographs which show, sorry, a further photograph which shows a focus on these two areas. So in the main this photograph shows their proximity. On this photograph you can see that the Muslim homes are totally destroyed and the mosque has been damaged. In the Serb section a short distance away you see the Orthodox Church totally intact and all the buildings totally intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, would you now refer to Exhibit 56C. Your Honours, we will be asking the usher to pass to your Honours copies of these photographs which you do not have in your collection. That, your Honours, is 56C. Mr. Ralston would you explain what 56C represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph of a village near Crska. You will see in this photograph the signs of houses which have been totally destroyed. I am advised that these houses were Muslim houses. Nestled in the middle of them here and here are two Serbian style homes which have suffered no damage at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I would now like to turn your attention to Exhibit No. 57, and ask you to identify what Exhibit 57 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 57 depicts for us the fate of many of the Muslim mosques throughout the Serb controlled areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Brcko in this site in early July 1992 we see a mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a graphic depiction of the mosque, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, of the mosque and the accompanying minaret. By May 1994 that area had been levelled completely. Not only had the mosque been destroyed, but any of the remnants of the mosque had been totally removed. I think the next exhibit will show that a little more graphically. This is the same area as I was pointing to in the previous exhibit, and this is the area where the mosque had stood. All traces have been removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, was there systematic destruction of religious sites in some of the locations that you have testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refer your Honours to Exhibit No. 58. We will display that on the elmo in just a minute. I will ask you, Mr. Ralston, to identify it and explain what it is once it comes up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This exhibit is a graphic representation of the Banja Luka area. It is significant in that Banja Luka was a Serbian majority population and, as such, there was no armed conflict in the area. Despite the fact there was no armed conflict in the area, many of the Muslim mosques were destroyed. This graphic plots the Muslim mosque locations and showed the ones that had been destroyed by September 1993. There are 14 depicted here in total, and since that graphic was prepared I am told that three further mosques have been destroyed and I am also told that that means the sum total of mosques in the Banja Luka area have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I would like now to turn to another feature of the pattern that you have identified in the municipalities where the Prosecutor's Office has conducted investigations, and that is the separation of men from women. Can you please explain that feature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have mentioned before in my testimony that men were separated from women. The men once they were separated were taken to detention facilities where they were held for weeks, months and even years. Some were then either deported to moved to other facilities or used in prisoner exchanges. The women were also often placed in detention facilities for various periods of time. In these facilities they were often subjected to persistent rape and sexual assault by camp officials and guards and soldiers, and on occasions civilians who came into the facilities. On other occasions people came into the facility, took women out, took them to various homes and locations where they were raped also. Other women were allowed to return to their homes. These women were often in an extremely vulnerable position. They were alone or with small children and no other support. They were at the peril of individuals and groups of soldiers who would visit unannounced and subject them to rape and sexual assault. They were also subjected to other types of threats and harassment which led many of them to take all the steps they could to escape from the area and the constant harassment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this pattern or this method of separating men from women occur only in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not, and this pattern repeated itself to certain extent as late as July 1995 when the Bosnian Serbs captured the Srebrenica safe area. After the fall of Srebrenica male refugees were separated from women and children. The women were then transported towards Tuzla. The males were taken to other locations and thousands of them were murdered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, would you please refer to Exhibit No. 59, identify it and explain its significance to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. This exhibit depicts in yellow the municipalities I have given testimony about. It shows the also the takeovers of the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa which were as late as July 1995. These municipalities, together with control of these municipalities which I have not give testimony about, or control of these municipalities, meant that the Bosnian Serbs controlled the area behind the confrontation line, and not only did they control it, they had a considerable ethnic majority in each of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified, Mr. Ralston, that many of the men and the women who were collected by the people who had taken over these communities were placed in detention facilities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please refer to Exhibit No. 60 and I will ask you to identify that and explain what it represents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This exhibit shows the location of some of the detention facilities that were set up in the areas controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. In the Prijedor area we have the Keraterm, Trnopolje, Omarska camps. There are also facilities in Sanski Most, Kljuc, Jajce, Kotor Varos. These camps tended to run by the civilian authorities and the police, although there was some involvement of the military. Manjaca was a totally military run camp. In this area again you have camps run by either the police or the military, and you have the Batkovic camp which is run strictly by the military. The arrows depict the movement of prisoners. Following the public outcry on the discovery of these camps, individuals were moved to the Manjaca camp. In relation to camps in this areas, as they closed down the detainees were moved to the Batkovic camp. Finally when Manjaca closed down in December 1992 some of the prisoners, I think about 500, from Manjaca were transferred to Batkovic. What this indicates is that the camps were not run in isolation. They were interconnected and people moved between each other. It also shows that detainees from the camps were moved from different areas of military control, from the area of the Drina Corps to the area of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, from the Krajina Corps to the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now are these camps still in existence, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge these camps have now been closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you now to focus your attention on those camps and ask you to describe the general conditions of the camps and what happened to the detainees who were inside them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The detainees in the camps, some were tortured, others were killed. Some were beaten during the takeover and held as human shields against possible resistance by armed Muslim groups. Women and men were separated in the camps, as I have testified. In Foca many of the women were being held around the partisan hall in various motels and apartments where they were subjected to rape an sexual assault. Our evidence shows that every evening the younger women and girls were taken out of the partisan sports hall in Foca, in the Foca high school, and were raped or ganged raped in rooms or apartments in neighbouring buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just described, Mr. Ralston, camps that were in the Foca municipality, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is what happened to the detainees in those camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention, please, to the camps that were located in the Vlasenica municipality and ask you the same question. Please describe the conditions of those camps and what occurred to the detainees in those camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Vlasenica people started to be detained between 2nd and 13th June. The main centre of detention was Susica camp. At Susica detainees were tortured, interrogated and beaten at random. Some died as a result of their beatings. The camp was located at the site of a former Territorial Defence storage centre. It ran from June 1992 to September 1992. There were so-called specialists who came in the camp and participated in the torturing of the detainees. When people arrived at the camp they were beaten, some so severely they died. Food was insufficient and most of the time inedible. As I have said before, the detainees in this camp were later transferred to Batkovic. I am told that in September 1992 when Susica camp closed about 200 detainees who remained there were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you please also describe to the Court what the conditions were like in the Prijedor camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Detention of civilians in Prijedor commenced shortly after the various military attacks. Civilians were rounded up the police, the military and the paramilitary forces. Detention facilities were run by the civil authorities staffed by police with some military guards. As I have said before, there were three main detention facilities: Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje. The conditions at the first two were particularly brutal. The Omarska camp opened at the end of May after the first attacks. It is a site of an iron ore mine. The camp was extremely crowded. Detainees were not permitted to move around freely. There was little water and what water there was often contaminated. The detention occurred in the summer. It was often very hot and the cramped the conditions and the heat compounded the human misery. There was no bedding provided for the inmates and there were few sanitary provisions. Those who ventured to use the sanitary provisions were beaten in the course of the attempt. Hygiene deteriorated and lice, diarrhoea and dysentery became prevalent. For the first three or four days in the camp there was little or no food. A small piece of bread and a small amount of a soup-like fluid are described as the main fare. All the detainees in Omarska lost a great deal of weight while at the camp. On arriving at the camp there were they were normally searched, their private possessions taken from them and not returned. They would then have to run the gauntlet of a cordon of guards who beat them with batons, clubs, rifle butts, kicking and punching them. Periodically guards demanded money and other valuable items from the prisoners. If they could not provide them beatings followed swiftly. There were a small number of women incarcerated at Omarska. With the exception of one, they were required to clean the interrogation rooms after inspectors had left for the day. They report that the rooms they were cleaning were often covered in blood and hair and skin which would have to be cleaned from the floor and walls. Weapons such as clubs electric cable, batons and similar instruments were kicked in the rooms. On an almost nightly basis some of these women were called from those rooms by the camp commanders, supervisors or guards, mistreated and sexually assaulted. I am told that the interrogations that were conducted in Omarska would involved somebody asking questions and at various stages through the interrogations other men coming into the room and inflicting brutal beatings on the person being interrogated. There were incidents of special terror which occurred. For example, on the eve the Petrovdan, a Serbian religious holiday in early July, to celebrate this festival the guards built a huge bonfire and engaged in a drinking spree. The detainees were dragged from their rooms, some were thrown alive into the fire, others were beaten severely. The screaming and crying of these victims created sheer terror for those people who were detained but fortunate enough not to be called out. In the latter part of July 1992 a large number of detainees who had been captured in the area of the left bank of the Sana River arrived in Omarska. This area was the last significant pocket of non-Serbs in the Prijedor municipality. After arrival in the camp they were subjected to brutal beatings and many of them were killed. As a result of the investigation carried out in relation to the activities of the guards in the Omarska camp two indictments have been issued by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, can you describe the conditions in the Manjaca detention facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Manjaca detention camp which was located 25 kilometres south of Banja Luka was run by the military. It was established in the summer of 1991 as a prisoner of war camp for Croatian prisoners of war of the war between Croatia and the FRY. From April to May 1992 the camp was used to detain non-Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina citizens. The camp was allegedly closed on 18th December 1992 when the last prisoners were moved to Batkovic or released to Karlovac in Croatia. The military ran the camp. The commanders were high ranked officers: a Lieutenant Colonel nicknamed Spaga and his successors, Lieutenant Colonel Bozidar Popovic, Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic and Lieutenant Colonel Bojic. Between June and August 1992 at least 3,600 people were detained at Manjaca camp. Almost all the detainees were men aged from their mid-teens to over 60. In December 1992 when the camp was closed approximately 2,500 people were released and 532 moved to other camps. From May to July the prisoners came from Doboj, Gornja Sanica, Sitnica, Stara Gradiska, Kljuc, Sanski Most, amongst others. After Omarska was closed in August 1992 prisoners came from that camp to Manjaca. After Jajce and Kotor Varos fell people were brought from those places to Manjaca. After August 1992 as a result of international media exposure and agreements concerning treatment of prisoners, many detainees were released or exchanged. On several occasions up to 1,000 people were moved to or from Manjaca. To move these large numbers of detainees across regional and municipal boundaries required significant organisation and co-ordination between police and military authorities. Many of the movements of detainees were as a direct result of agreements made by Karadzic and show the extent of command and control he exercised in relation to the detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I have asked you to prepare selected film clips showing the condition of detainees in Omarska and Trnopolje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we could, please -- actually before we slow the clip, Mr. Ralston, would you please inform the Court what they will see on the film before it is shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This film was taken at the beginning of August 1992 shortly after the international community became aware of the existence of the camps. You will see clips taken at Trnopolje and Omarska. The footage taken at Omarska will depict emaciated detainees hungrily attacking food which I have been told was in access of that normally provided to them. You will observe them almost eat the enamel off the plate they are eating from. In contrast you will see an armed and apparently well-fed guard overseeing the detainees while they eat. From that clip we move to a clip of the Trnopolje detention facility. The detainees depicted in this clip had recently been transferred from Omarska and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if we could show, please, film clip No. 3 Exhibit No. 29. Can we dim the lights as well. Thank you. (Exhibit 29 clip No. 3 was shown). Your Honour, I notice it is a little past 5.30. I have one more question to ask Mr. Ralston and then I will conclude my examination for the day. Mr. Ralston, did Dr. Karadzic ever comment about the images that have been shown on these films?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic has repeatedly been asked about these camps. An example of his response to such questions was published in the Independent Magazine in London. Karadzic said: "When they started talking about the concentration camps I happened to be in London. I told them, 'I don't know what the condition are like in those camps. We do keep prisoners. We do not kill them. We must keep them. It is war. So, Penny Marshall, an ITN journalist, came to Ormaska and picked out a few very skinny guys who will never look better. When I was 30 I too looked like them. She presented that to the world."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no additional evidence for the day, your Honour. We have concluded our presentation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Ralston. Thank you Prosecutor. So we will stand in recess this Friday evening. We will resume Monday at 10 o'clock. (The court adjourned until Monday, 1st July 1996) 20 21 22 23 24 25
